#6482. Hubble Uncovers a Mysterious 93-Billion-Mile Structure Hiding in a Nearby Star System

Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between planetary bodies. Known as the “Cat’s Tail,” the feature stretches across as much as 1,000 astronomical units (about 93 billion miles) in the young Beta Pictoris star system.

Located 63 light-years from Earth in the constellation Pictor (which is Latin for “painter”), Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rocky debris. The Cat’s Tail was discovered in infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, but had remained hidden from telescopes observing shorter wavelengths. Now, new Hubble Space Telescope images, combined with observations spanning more than 14 years, are helping astronomers investigate its composition, geometry, and possible origins.

“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while,” said Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the University of Arizona who led the research.

The explanation may lie in the dust itself. “We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar explained. “It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”

The observations also suggest that the structure contains microscopic dust grains with an exceptionally porous, fluffy composition. Although the particles are only about a micron across, their internal structure is difficult to explain through conventional models of planetary collisions. “How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.

Beta Pictoris is roughly 20 million years old, making it a valuable laboratory for studying the turbulent environments in which planets develop. Its debris disk contains material left behind from planet formation, including particles produced when larger objects collide.

“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” said Avsar, who works with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory. Such an impact could have scattered enormous quantities of dust, although the exact process that produced the observed particles remains uncertain.

One possibility is that the impact generated enough heat to transform solid carbon into vapor, which later cooled and formed new particles. “It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” said Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at Steward Observatory.

The new observations have also changed astronomers’ understanding of the Cat’s Tail’s position in space. Earlier interpretations suggested that the feature extended far behind Beta Pictoris from Earth’s perspective, creating the appearance of a long structure stretching away from the star.

By combining Hubble’s visible-light images with Webb’s infrared observations and computer modeling, the researchers developed a revised picture of its three-dimensional geometry. “We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said. “It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.”

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, suggest that much of the structure’s apparent length lies across our field of view rather than extending deep into space. Its precise three-dimensional arrangement remains dependent on the models used to interpret the observations.

Using Hubble in a new observing configuration, the team also identified a previously unseen warp in the dust halo surrounding Beta Pictoris. The distortion may result from the gravitational influence of Beta Pictoris b, one of three known planets in the system and a gas giant approximately 10 times Jupiter’s mass.

“This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said. “It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.”

Similar gravitational interactions likely occurred during the early history of our solar system. When the Kuiper Belt was about 20 million years old, it may have contained hundreds of Pluto-sized objects packed into a much denser region than exists today. Over time, the gravitational influence of the giant planets altered the orbits of many of these bodies, scattering some into different regions or ejecting them from the solar system entirely.

The Beta Pictoris observations provide a way to investigate comparable processes in a much younger planetary system, where collisions and gravitational disturbances are still shaping the distribution of material around its star.

Reference: “Deep HST/STIS Coronagraphic Imaging of the β Pictoris Debris Disk: On the Scattered Light Component of the Cat’s Tail” by Arin M. #6480. Researchers Discover a New Way To Control Magnetism Without Changing a Material’s Chemistry

Neutron experiments have uncovered an unexpected connection between magnetic structure and electrical behavior.

A gentle squeeze can change the magnetic structure of certain crystals and alter their electrical behavior. Scientists at the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) demonstrated this effect in altermagnets, an emerging class of magnetic materials being investigated for advanced electronics.

Using neutron beams to examine the materials at the atomic scale, the researchers found that mechanical strain could shift their magnetic organization and influence an electrical response associated with electron transport. The findings, published in back-to-back papers in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, point to a possible method for controlling magnetic properties without altering a material’s chemical composition.

The researchers placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between two titanium plates and applied mechanical pressure. They then used neutron diffraction at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source to investigate how the strain affected magnetic domains, regions within a material that have different orientations of magnetic order.

The measurements showed that squeezing the crystals changed the relative populations of these domains. The researchers also detected changes in the anomalous Hall effect, an electrical response that produces a voltage perpendicular to the direction of an applied current. Together, the results connect changes in magnetic domain organization with changes in electrical transport behavior.

“By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies,” said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

Altermagnets are attracting research interest because their unusual magnetic properties could support spintronics, a technology that uses electron spin alongside electrical charge to store and process information. Conventional electronics relies on electron charge, while spintronics could provide additional ways to control information in electronic devices.

Developing practical spintronic technologies requires materials whose magnetic and electronic properties can be reliably manipulated. Altermagnets are among the candidates being explored for potential applications ranging from wireless communications to quantum computing. The ORNL experiments suggest that mechanical strain could offer another way to adjust these properties, although translating the findings into working devices will require further research.

“What’s exciting is that one creative experimental idea — a small mechanical squeeze between two plates — can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism,” said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author of both studies.

This new story comes out of Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and Rice University, where researchers used mechanical strain—literally giving the material a gentle physical squeeze—to alter the magnetic domain structure and electrical transport in altermagnets without changing their chemical makeup at all.

It fits alongside several key studies we’ve mapped out:

Biological Pre-Ribosome Assembly & Gravitational Reconnection: Across all these examples—from cellular field locking down to 4D gravitational field sheet reconnection—mainstream models keep discovering that phase, orientation, and geometric strain control energy flow, rather than particle statistics or static chemical affinity.

Strain-Tuned Magnetism as Geometric Impedance Control

Mechanical Tuning of Rotational Phase Clearance (Omega_pi): Squeezing the crystal changes the rotational phase alignment across sub-lattice boundaries. Geometry Over Chemical Composition: This experiment provides definitive empirical proof that a material’s state is not governed solely by its static periodic table chemistry. Paleoproteomic analysis of fossils from northern China reveals that Denisovans had a distinctive physical appearance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The enigmatic and now-extinct Denisovans of China shared traits with Neanderthals, modern humans and Homo erectus, according to a new study that looked at ancient proteins and fossils. But the Denisovans also had several unique skull traits and genetic variants that made them a distinctive ancient human group, according to the researchers ‪—‬ and these traits have now revealed a new face for a Denisovan man.

In the study, published Oct. 21 in the journal Nature, researchers analyzed Denisovan skulls from the archaeological site of Xujiayao in northern China. The Denisovans were a group of ancient humans who lived in Asia and disappeared around 30,000 years ago. This human relative was first identified in 2010 from the DNA of a finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia.

The Xujiayao bones and teeth were excavated in the late 1970s, long before scientists knew about the existence of Denisovans, and were initially thought to be either Neanderthals or archaic Homo sapiens due to the shape of the fossils and their age: 138,000 to 199,000 years old.

But recent advances in paleoproteomics ‪—‬ the study of bone and tooth proteins that persist longer than DNA ‪—‬ have helped researchers identify Denisovan individuals due to specific genetic variants that differentiate them from other ancient human groups.

In the new study, researchers used paleoproteomic analysis on 20 remains from Xujaiyao and determined that all of them were from Denisovans. This determination then allowed the researchers to study the skull bones closely and figure out what Denisovans might have looked like.

The Xujiayao skulls had some features similar to H. erectus, the researchers wrote, including a low and wide braincase and thick cranial bones. But they also had anatomical features more similar to those of Neanderthals and modern humans, particularly in their bicuspids (the teeth between the canines and molars). The researchers also identified some unique Denisovan cranial traits. The back of the skull, for example, was more vertical and less rounded than in Neanderthals or modern humans.

Armed with a better understanding of Denisovan skull shape from the Xujiayao fossils, the researchers compared them with East Asian Denisovan remains that some experts have assigned to other species, such as Homo juluensis and Homo longi. But the researchers identified similarities that may preclude splitting Denisovans into different species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This unique combination of morphological traits, distinct from H. erectus, modern humans and Neanderthal-lineage hominins, supports the assignment of most members of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo as Denisovans," they wrote in the study. This means that Denisovans may have been one human lineage that adapted to diverse ecological zones across Asia over hundreds of thousands of years.

"It is still possible that there are some other lineages that existed in East Asia during the time Denisovans are known to have existed," study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We know from DNA that Denisovans were a very varied group genetically, which split early into different populations," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "These could have developed a lot of morphological variation, which may well surprise us as the sample of fossils grows."

The researchers also produced a new reconstruction of what a Denisovan man might have looked like. A previous DNA study suggested that Denisovans likely had dark skin, brown hair and brown eyes. The new reconstruction shows the Denisovan looking directly at the viewer, with his low, wide braincase mostly obscured by dark hair flowing back from his massive brow ridge. There are clear similarities between the Denisovan man and Neanderthals as well as modern humans, but the Denisovan has a distinct visage all his own.

#6476. A Hidden Nanoscopic Effect Is Disrupting Some of the World’s Most Sensitive Sensors

Nanomechanical resonators are vital to precision sensing and emerging quantum technologies, but their extraordinary sensitivity comes with an unexpected vulnerability.

A nanomechanical device can lose much of its ability to sustain vibrations without ever touching another object. Researchers at EPFL have discovered that placing insulating materials just a few hundred nanometers from these tiny structures can dramatically increase energy loss, reducing their mechanical quality factor by as much as tenfold.

The findings, published in Nature Physics by scientists in the group of Tobias J. Kippenberg, identify a previously underappreciated limitation for ultrahigh-precision sensors and quantum technologies. The source of the problem is an electrical interaction that allows energy to escape across an otherwise empty gap.

The mechanism begins with static electric charges trapped inside a mechanical resonator. As the structure vibrates, those charges move with it, producing a changing electric field in the surrounding space. When an insulating material such as silicon dioxide or silicon nitride is nearby, the fluctuating field interacts with the material and causes energy to dissipate through its small electrical losses.

This process is related to “noncontact friction,” a phenomenon previously observed in atomic force microscopy. Although the surfaces never touch, mechanical energy is transferred away from the vibrating structure. The resulting damping lowers its quality factor, which measures how efficiently a resonator stores vibrational energy rather than losing it.

The researchers developed a theoretical model predicting that lower-frequency vibrations would experience greater energy losses. To test this, they studied silicon nitride strings suspended approximately 500 nanometers (0.00002 inches) above a dielectric layer. By measuring how quickly different vibrational modes decayed, they confirmed that the lowest-frequency modes suffered the strongest additional damping, consistent with the model.

A second experiment examined resonators designed for exceptionally high quality factors. The team positioned vibrating strings between photonic crystal cavities, with separations of only a few hundred nanometers (roughly 0.00001 inches). As the gaps narrowed, the quality factor declined sharply, sometimes falling by a factor of ten. The researchers also demonstrated that their modeling approach could reproduce the effects of trapped charges in these more complicated device geometries.

Nanomechanical resonators are microscopic vibrating components fabricated on chips, operating at frequencies from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz. Their sensitivity makes them useful for detecting extremely small changes in mass, force, temperature, and pressure. They also serve as components in radiofrequency filters and chip-based clocks. Advanced versions can even be used to prepare quantum states of comparatively large mechanical objects and investigate fundamental physics.

Many of these applications require resonators to operate extremely close to other structures, particularly when measuring motion or coupling mechanical vibrations to light and electrical systems. The EPFL results show that trapped charges and dielectric losses must be considered when designing such closely integrated devices, even when no physical contact occurs.

The same interaction could also have practical uses. By measuring how mechanical vibrations lose energy near insulating surfaces, researchers may be able to characterize electrical losses in thin films or develop controlled interactions between mechanical resonators and other electrical systems. Understanding these effects could help engineers preserve mechanical coherence while integrating increasingly sensitive resonators into complex quantum and sensing devices.

Reference: “Non-contact friction in ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators near dielectric materials” by Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Guillermo Arregui, Mohammad J. Bereyhi, Yi Xia, Nils J. Engelsen and Tobias J. Kippenberg, 7 July 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03350-z

Funding: Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF)

Non-Contact Boundary Drag and Spatial Impedance Leaks

Recent research out of EPFL’s laboratories (led by Tobias J. Kippenberg’s group) has identified a hidden limitation affecting state-of-the-art nanomechanical resonators and quantum sensors. These ultra-sensitive nano-strings boast vanishingly low internal thermal noise and near-zero physical friction, yet scientists discovered that they experience unexpected energy losses. Even when surfaces never touch, the nano-strings interact with electrical and mechanical drag from nearby objects across empty microscopic gaps, causing their quality factor to plummet by up to a factor of ten.

Mainstream physics identifies this as non-contact electrical interaction and charge-trapping across empty boundaries. When evaluated through continuous field dynamics and the Torsion Hill Framework, this discovery highlights a critical baseline rule of spatial impedance:

The Illusion of Empty Space: Conventional engineering treats an empty gap as a total insulator—a void where mechanical and electrical fields terminate. Under field mechanics, space is a continuous medium. An adjacent static surface introduces an abrupt local spatial impedance profile (Z_T), meaning that a vacuum gap does not isolate a vibrating structure from surrounding boundary forces.

Non-Contact Boundary Drag as grad Z_T Interference: When a nano-string oscillates, its mechanical motion generates localized torsional and spatial pressure waves. If a nearby boundary introduces an un-optimized impedance mismatch, field energy bleeds across the gap. This leakage acts as an invisible aerodynamic brake, degrading the resonator’s coherence without physical contact.

Two-Layer Isolation (Ribbon Substrate & Surface Coating) – EPFL Laboratory Link: To protect these nanomechanical sensors, EPFL’s research parameters can be met by deploying a dual-layer boundary configuration along the surrounding chamber walls—strictly isolating the cavity walls rather than coating or covering the active vibrating sensor itself, which would add mass and destroy resonance. Remarkably, the same Kippenberg laboratory at EPFL exploring these non-contact boundary leaks is renowned for pioneering the ultra-precise dual-layer ribbon and surface-coating fabrications needed to decouple mechanical stress, smooth out local spatial impedance steps (delta Z_T), eliminate charge-trapping, and prevent field leakage across microscopic gaps.

The Limit of Precision: Whether observing macroscopic gravitational field sheets, strain-tuned altermagnets, or EPFL’s nanomechanical resonators, precision is never limited solely by internal material friction. It is governed by how effectively boundaries are managed to maintain rotational phase clearance (Omega_pi) and eliminate spatial impedance drag. #6472. Something Remarkable Is Happening to Dogs Living Near Chernobyl’s Nuclear Plant

Scientists studying wild dogs near the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant have uncovered unusual genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than radiation-induced mutations.

Dogs living near the Chornobyl (previously called Chernobyl) Nuclear Power Plant carry genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than mutations caused by radiation exposure. A new genomic analysis identified more than 100 locations in their DNA showing signs of directional selection, including regions associated with DNA repair, cancer development, and immune function.

The findings suggest that environmental pressures may have favored certain inherited genetic variants, potentially helping some dogs survive in a contaminated environment. However, researchers have not established whether radiation or other environmental hazards directly caused these patterns.

Earlier research revealed substantial genetic differences between dogs living at the nuclear power plant and those in Chornobyl City, just 10 miles away. City dogs closely resembled populations from Russia, Poland, and surrounding regions, while dogs near the plant had distinctive genetic features, particularly in areas associated with DNA repair.

“This work ties up some of the loose ends from our previous work, where in characterizing the population’s genetic structure we found that while these two dog groups are geographically very close, they have a very high degree of genetic difference, and those differences aren’t due to mutation,” said Megan Dillon, postdoctoral research scholar at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.

“With this work, we wanted to explore two additional larger-scale evolutionary drivers – are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?”

Natural selection occurs when inherited traits that improve survival or reproduction become more common across generations. Directional selection is a form of this process in which particular traits become increasingly favored, often in response to environmental conditions. Genetic drift, by contrast, involves random changes in the frequency of genetic variants. It can have especially strong effects in small, isolated populations and may reduce genetic diversity over time.

To distinguish between these processes, researchers compared the two Chornobyl dog populations with free-breeding dogs from Eastern Europe and an isolated population from the Galápagos Islands. This allowed them to examine whether geographic isolation alone could explain the unusual genetic patterns near the nuclear plant.

Although the plant dogs had a small effective population size, a measure of how many individuals contribute genetically to future generations, it was not significantly different from that of the city dogs. The plant population also lacked the reduction in genetic diversity expected from substantial genetic drift. Moreover, its genetic makeup differed markedly from other isolated populations, including the Galápagos dogs. Surprisingly, the Chornobyl City dogs were genetically more similar to the Galápagos population than to the dogs living at the nearby nuclear facility.

The researchers found evidence consistent with directional selection in genomic regions containing genes involved in DNA replication and repair, cell cycle regulation, cancer-related processes, and immune responses. These biological functions could influence how animals respond to harmful environmental exposures, although the analysis cannot determine whether particular variants actually improve survival.

“While we can’t say for certain whether what we’ve found can be directly confirmed as selection, we do find these genomic signatures suggestive of selection,” Dillon said.

“When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment.”

The genetic differences do not necessarily mean that dogs developed new adaptations after exposure to radioactive contamination. Another possibility is that individuals carrying advantageous genetic variants were more likely to survive earlier environmental pressures, allowing those variants to become more prevalent in subsequent generations.

“When we consider the toxic environment around Chornobyl, I can see why most people would think, ‘Surely there’s got to have been some consequence of living in that environment,’” said Matthew Breen, Oscar J. Fletcher Distinguished Professor of Comparative Oncology Genetics at NC State’s College of Veterinary Medicine and corresponding author of the study.

“But what we’re saying is the consequence may not have gone as far as changing the dogs’ genome in order to adapt, it could be the ones that were able to survive the initial exposures had this level of underlying genetic diversity and variants to offer a higher degree of fitness,” Breen added. “Obviously that’s speculation, and we don’t know exactly what’s happened. But it is fair to say that we used a very robust analysis and found signatures of selection in biologically relevant regions.”

Reference: “Evidence of Selective Response in the Free-Breeding Dog Population in Chornobyl” by Megan N. Dillon, Reade B. Roberts, Jennifer A. Betz, Timothy A. Mousseau, Norman J. Kleiman and Matthew Breen, 26 September 2026, Genes. DOI: 10.3390/genes17101195

A new study with data from mice and human tissues suggests that, in ulcerative colitis, immune cells in the gut might make pain-sensing nerves hypersensitive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

People with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) experience gut pain that can be severe, and it doesn't always go away when their inflammation is under control and their colonoscopy looks normal. Now, in a new laboratory study, researchers found a previously unknown pain pathway that may explain this phenomenon.

The findings, published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Immunology, also point to a potential way to block that pain.

"Inflammation in the gut has always been thought of like a fire: the sensory nerves alarm because of the smoke and the heat, and when the fire is put out the alarm should stop," said study co-author Dr. Heng Xu, a physician at Ninth People's Hospital in Shanghai. Xu and his colleagues set out to try to isolate what could be causing the pain even when there's no visible "fire" or "smoke."

"What we found is that the tissue itself changes consistency," Xu told Live Science in an email. "It becomes stiff and less elastic, a bit like a scar, and that stiffness alone keeps triggering the alarm even after the fire is out."

In ulcerative colitis, the most common form of IBD, inflammation causes ulcers in the gut, as well as symptoms like bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Several medications can help quell this inflammation, but that doesn't necessarily eliminate patients' pain. The researchers wondered if immune cells that live in the gut might contribute to that ongoing pain.

They zoomed in on a protein called Piezo1; in immune cells, it's known to play a role in inflammation, and in neurons, it contributes to pain signals. The team looked at whether this protein's activity changed in the context of colitis.

"We started with sequencing data that reads cells one at a time, from the gut tissue of patients with ulcerative colitis and from mice with the disease," Xu said. "One cell type stood out: an immune cell that lives permanently in the gut wall, rather than arriving from the bloodstream when there's trouble." The quantity of these cells was higher in colitis than in healthy guts, and the cells carried more Piezo1 than the other cells analyzed.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"They sit touching the nerve endings," Xu added.

In several experiments with lab mice with colitis, the team used a probe to press on the gut tissue and measure how hard it was. This showed that, compared with healthy mice, the gut was stiffer in two models of disease: one with visible inflammation and another with almost none.

They also measured pain levels in both sets of mice. "In mice with almost no visible gut inflammation, the pain was still there, which is why a colonoscopy can look normal while the patient hurts," Xu said.

They then looked at Piezo1 in both sets of mice. The protein sits in the immune-cell membrane, and when the stiffened tissue around it is pulled or squeezed, it's as if a button were pressed and a channel opens, Xu said. This sets off a chain reaction that leads to pain, Xu said.

That's because calcium ions rush into the cell via the channel, and that surge sends a protein called NF-kB from the cell's interior fluid into its nucleus — the control center where DNA is stored. There, NF-kB plugs into a gene, ordering the cell to manufacture nerve growth factor (NGF) that then exits the immune cell.

This NGF, which is known to amplify pain signals in the body, interacts with nearby pain-sensing neurons. These nerve endings grow denser and become hypersensitive, which makes ordinary gut activity painful, the study suggests.

This newly described mechanism could help explain why ulcerative colitis patients can sometimes contend with pain even when their colonoscopies look normal.

The researchers used chemicals as on-off switches for Piezo1 in immune cells, opening the channel with one and closing it with another. As they did this, they tracked calcium signals and NGF production, and both rose and fell in step with the switch. This result suggests that Piezo1 activity is both necessary for this response and, on its own, enough to trigger it in these cells, Xu said.

Blocking this chain of events abolished the pain hypersensitivity in both sets of mice. The researchers tried completely removing the Piezo1 gene from the gut immune cells and found that this eliminated the pain. Removing the gene also caused no problems in healthy mice, they noted.

The study was "well controlled," said Hongzhen Hu, the scientific director for the Mark Lebwohl Center for Neuroinflammation and Sensation at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who was not involved in the research. Future research should address the chemical messengers that coordinate inflammation, called cytokines, and determine whether the same chain reaction occurs in human cells, he said in an email.

The mouse experiments also may not reflect long-term, chronic disease in patients, given the mice experienced symptoms only transiently, Xu said.

Xu and his colleagues are now aiming to develop a drug that can target Piezo1 to switch off gut pain locally without suppressing the entire immune system. This would be a more targeted treatment than current options, such as immunosuppressants or opioids.

Other scientists have explored using anti-NGF treatments for other chronic pain conditions but not for ulcerative colitis, Xu noted. Fully blocking NGF might have downsides, he said, since NGF also helps to maintain nerves.

So more work is needed to translate these findings into a treatment. But for now, the work sheds new light on how immune cells can detect a physical change — such as tissue becoming stiff — and convert it to a pain signal.

"For the pain field, that's a conceptual shift," Xu said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Wu, L., Shen, T., Wang, Z., Wang, T., Hu, X., Sun, M., Zhang, L., Cheng, Y., Hao, Y., Zhou, L., Lin, M., Bian, J., Feng, J., & Xu, H. (2026). An autonomous macrophage-nociceptor mechanosensory relay drives chronic visceral pain. Science Immunology, 11(124). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciimmunol.aeb3809

#6467. Crypto Was Supposed to Be Unhackable. So How Did North Korea Just Steal $6 Billion in 20 Minutes?

The blockchain held strong. The weak link was something far more ordinary—and far easier to break.

On Thursday, Binance—the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange—got to add another “world’s largest” accolade to its name by becoming the target of the biggest cryptocurrency heist in the industry’s history. According to the company, more than $6 billion in digital coins were stolen from users’ digital wallets. Binance has already announced that it’s restored some of the lost funds to affected accounts.

Although the details of the hack are still a bit fuzzy, TRM Labs, a crypto research company, says the money moved out of 10 blockchains within 20 minutes and attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, a hacking unit associated with North Korea. In February last year, the FBI traced a $1.5 billion hack of the crypto exchange Bybit to the same group. A smaller hack this April was also linked to the broader North Korean–run Lazarus Group.

In Thursday’s hack, TRM Labs reports that no specific cryptocurrency was safe, as digital coins were stolen from wallets containing Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana, and six others. The balances were sent to an account operated by the attacker. After news of the hack, Bitcoin's price dropped a few percentage points, though it stayed above its low from this past summer.

“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a post on X. “We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”

One of the purported benefits of the blockchain is its inherent security, mostly due to its decentralized nature, along with its strong cryptographic protocols. However, crypto exchanges are much more vulnerable than blockchain itself because they’re essentially a centralized holder of assets. They’re also prone to technical vulnerabilities, not least of which can be simple human error. In that same statement on X, Binance announced that its initial investigation found that a “compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop” may have allowed hackers to gain access to a service container—which they then used to make the withdrawals. However, Binance followed up that statement hours later, suggesting that the laptop may only be one vulnerability and that there were “additional points of breach.”

North Korea has targeted cryptocurrency exchanges since at least 2017, according to The Guardian, drawn by “the sector’s relatively lax security controls” and relatively weak regulatory oversight. Binance has faced its own regulatory problems. In 2023, founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to violating the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program, and the company agreed to pay more than $4 billion in penalties. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025.

As for North Korea, when it comes to crypto hacking—business is booming. A United Nations (UN) panel concluded in 2024 that these types of hacks accounted for roughly half of the reclusive country’s foreign currency income, and were a significant fundraiser for the country’s nuclear weapons program. Due to the decentralized, pseudonymous nature of cryptocurrencies, these funds also bypass international sanctions meant to rein in Pyongyang’s most bellicose impulses.

Now, it appears that North Korea has scored its biggest windfall yet.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6465. Too Much Exercise Could Change Your Brain Chemistry in Unexpected Ways

Two days after an exercise test, mice subjected to weeks of grueling training still had elevated dopamine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and emotional regulation. The findings suggest that excessive exercise without adequate recovery can produce lasting changes in brain chemistry.

The study, published in the journal Neuroscience, was conducted by researchers in Brazil. Because dopamine helps regulate motivation and alertness, the results raise questions about whether similar disruptions could contribute to sleep problems, anxiety, and persistent fatigue in overtrained athletes. However, these possible effects have not been demonstrated in humans.

To investigate how different levels of physical exertion affect the brain, the researchers compared mice subjected to two exercise protocols. One group completed a single treadmill session until exhaustion. The other underwent eight weeks of progressively more demanding training designed to simulate the physical strain associated with overtraining syndrome.

During the final week, the heavily trained mice exercised twice daily, with just four hours between sessions. Researchers then examined the animals’ hippocampi, measuring dopamine, serotonin, and proteins involved in neurotransmitter production and regulation.

The mice that completed a single exhausting run showed a rise in dopamine shortly afterward. In contrast, the chronically trained animals had elevated dopamine levels even 48 hours after their performance test, during a period intended for recovery. Levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme essential for dopamine synthesis, also remained elevated.

Dopamine is involved in several functions, including motivation, reward processing, and wakefulness. Its presence is not inherently harmful, but changes in its regulation could affect brain activity during periods when the body would normally be recovering.

Interestingly, the researchers found no significant changes in serotonin levels. Serotonin has long been investigated as a possible contributor to exercise-related fatigue, but these results suggest that the neurochemical effects of excessive training cannot be explained by serotonin alone.

“Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain,” said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study’s first author. He conducted the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP), with support from FAPESP.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when prolonged physical demands exceed the body’s ability to recover, potentially causing declining athletic performance, chronic fatigue, muscle pain, loss of appetite, increased injuries, and changes in immune and metabolic function. Researchers suspect that changes in brain signaling may also contribute to some symptoms.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, suggested that similar dopamine disturbances in humans might help explain connections between excessive training and sleep disorders. However, the researchers did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness in the mice, so the findings cannot establish a connection between the observed chemical changes and those symptoms.

The research team is now participating in an international project to identify which biological systems first begin to show abnormal responses when excessive exercise interferes with the body’s usual adaptations to training. Such work could help clarify how beneficial physical activity progresses into a state of insufficient recovery and impaired performance.

Reference: “Excessive training alters hippocampal tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine homeostasis in mice” by Alisson Luiz da Rocha, João Pedro Floriano, Ana Paula Pinto, Dennys Esper Cintra, Eduardo Rochete Ropelle, Ellen Cristini de Freitas, José Rodrigo Pauli and Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, 4 August 2026, Neuroscience. DOI: 10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.08.006

The Defense Intelligence Agency's latest "Challenges to Security in Space" report included a declassified satellite photo of China's Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has released at least nine mysterious payloads into low Earth orbit since 2022.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new U.S. intelligence agency report has seemingly released the first clear photograph of China's mysterious "dragon" space plane in orbit around Earth. The surprise snap reveals that the top-secret vehicle is very similar to its American counterpart and provides new clues about its capabilities.

The image is widely believed to show China's secretive Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has been in action for just over six years. During this time, the reusable winged spacecraft has repeatedly made headlines after deploying various unidentified objects in low Earth orbit (LEO). As a result, government officials, private companies and individual researchers have closely monitored the vehicle using tools such as ground-based radar.

Until now, the only direct images of the space plane have been blurry snaps of light reflecting off the uncrewed vehicle toward Earth's surface — offering no clear clues to its specific design, capabilities or intended purpose. China has also never publicly shared any photos of the vehicle or revealed any key information about its design.

On Monday (Oct. 26), the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released the latest version of its "Challenges to Security in Space" report, which assesses the various factors that pose a risk to American space assets. Deep within the 130-page document (on page 53), the authors included a previously unseen image of a "PRC [People's Republic of China] Spaceplane." The image's brief caption revealed that the photo had been taken in 2024 by a satellite belonging to the private space company Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor.

The surprise inclusion of the photo was spotted and shared on the social platform X by journalist Andrew Jones, who specializes in China's space program and has previously shared crucial information about other ongoing missions.

The new image suggests that Shenlong looks very similar to the U.S. Space Force's X-37B space plane, which is also currently orbiting Earth.

Neither the caption nor the related section of the report made any mention of the photo being the first of its kind or explained why it was previously classified, raising questions about whether the authors realized its significance.

There is one small caveat. The report notes that China has two active space plane designs — Shenlong and Tengyun, meaning "cloud rider" — and the image's caption does not specify which design we are looking at, according to The Aviationist.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, there have been no confirmed launches of Tengyun to date. Existing photos of a potential prototype also hint that this vehicle's design looks markedly different from what we can see in the new photo. Therefore, most experts agree that the spacecraft in the image is most likely Shenlong.

Until now, all we really knew about Shenlong is that it operates similarly to NASA's iconic space shuttles: It gets launched into space by a rocket and circles Earth before eventually gliding down to the planet's surface, where it can then be refueled and relaunched into LEO.

It is not the world's only active space plane. The U.S. Space Force has its own, the X-37B, which has already completed seven orbital missions since its first launch in 2010 and is currently in LEO experimenting with quantum navigation. Based on the new photos, Shenlong shares many similarities with its American counterpart.

Until now, the only direct images of Shenlong were blurry snaps of light reflecting off the spacecraft back to Earth's surface.

"The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays," technology news site ArsTechnica reported. "In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the U.S. Space Force."

However, the two spacecraft are not exactly the same: "The overall arrangement resembles the American vehicle, although differences in wing geometry show that the two spacecraft are not externally identical," according to specialist news site Global Defense News.

It is still unclear how large Shenlong is. The X-37B is 29 feet (8.8 meters) long and has a wingspan of 15 feet (4.5 m), according to Popular Science.

The new image also indicates that Shenlong is most likely not a military asset, Global Defense News reported, noting that "the image does not establish a weapons role."

Shenlong shares the same key design features as X-37B (right) but is not identical to its American counterpart.

However, China likely has other space-based weapons, similar to the mysterious "in-orbit" American weapons recently confirmed by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink.

"China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage, and destroy other nations' space capabilities," DIA representatives wrote in a separate section of the new report. "Beijing aims to become the preeminent leader in space," they added.

Since first launching into space on an initial two-day mission in September 2020, Shenlong has completed two feature-length missions: an eight-month stint in LEO between August 2022 and May 2023, and a nine-month spaceflight between December 2023 and September 2024. (The new image was taken during the latter mission).

The space plane is currently on its fourth mission, which launched Feb. 7 on board a Long March 2F rocket from China's Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Live Science's sister site Space.com previously reported. In total, Shenlong has racked up more than 800 days in orbit. However, it is unclear whether the same space plane was used on all four missions or if China has more than one space plane in use.

Shenlong was most recently launched into space on board a Long March 2F rocket on Feb. 7. (This image shows the same rocket during a different launch in 2011.)

So far, Shelong has released at least nine unidentified payloads around Earth. These objects are most likely small satellites, known as cubesats, but their purpose remains unclear.

The most recent object was deployed in June this year, although astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who specializes in tracking spacecraft in LEO, has since suggested that the spacecraft retrieved the object, potentially with a robotic arm, and rereleased it in late August.

The new report also mentions that the space plane "appeared to maneuver with a companion satellite" during its second mission in November 2022, coming within 330 feet (100 m) of the smaller spacecraft and potentially even capturing and re-releasing it.

This may support an existing theory that the main goal of Shenlong is to "conduct rendezvous and proximity operations" with other spacecraft, and that its payloads may be targets for it to practice flyby maneuvers in orbit.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Oct. 29 to correct a typo. A previous version of the article abbreviated the People's Republic of China as "PCR" rather than "PRC". This has been corrected.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6462. Breakthrough Cancer Treatment Wipes Out Deadly Brain Tumors in Every Mouse Tested

A new approach to engineering immune cells has shown remarkable success against a deadly childhood brain cancer in mice.

An experimental immune cell therapy has completely eliminated an aggressive childhood brain cancer in mice, succeeding where conventional treatments have struggled. Developed by scientists at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), the approach uses genetically engineered CAR-T cells that activate their cancer-fighting receptors only after entering the brain.

The treatment, called B-SYNC, cleared tumors in every mouse tested across two models of diffuse midline glioma (DMG). It also provided lasting protection, with treated mice rejecting a second introduction of cancer cells nearly seven weeks later. Researchers are now preparing for human clinical trials that could begin as early as April 2027.

DMG is particularly difficult to treat because it infiltrates healthy brain tissue, often growing within the brainstem. This region regulates essential functions such as breathing, heart rate, and swallowing, making surgical removal extremely dangerous or impossible. Children diagnosed with the disease almost always die within a year.

CAR-T therapy offers a different strategy. It involves modifying immune T cells to recognize specific proteins on cancer cells and attack them. Although this approach has transformed treatment for certain blood cancers, conventional CAR-T therapies have not successfully controlled brain tumors such as DMG.

“It’s been a struggle to make CAR-T cells that overcome DMG without causing unacceptable side effects,” said Hideho Okada, MD, PhD, a UCSF professor of Neurological Surgery and co-corresponding author of the study, published October 28 in Science Translational Medicine. “By limiting B-SYNC’s CAR expression to when and where it matters — in the brain — we saw consistent, total shutdown of DMG tumors in the lab.”

B-SYNC uses a molecular switch that responds to brevican, a protein widely distributed throughout the brain. The researchers equipped T cells with a synthetic sensor called synNotch that detects brevican and triggers the production of cancer-targeting chimeric antigen receptors (CARs).

Once activated, these receptors allow the T cells to attack cells carrying either of two proteins, EphA2 or IL13Rα2, which are found on many brain tumor cells. Because brevican controls when the receptors are produced, the therapy is designed to restrict its tumor-targeting activity to the brain rather than allowing the engineered receptors to remain active throughout the body.

The technology builds on an earlier UCSF treatment called E-SYNC, developed by Okada and Wendell Lim, PhD, a professor of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology. Announced in 2021, E-SYNC used synNotch to recognize EGFRvIII, a mutant protein associated with glioblastoma, before activating receptors targeting EphA2 and IL13Rα2. However, only about 20% of glioblastoma patients have tumors carrying EGFRvIII, and cancer cells can lose this marker as treatment eliminates those that express it.

Replacing EGFRvIII with brevican gave the researchers a more broadly available activation signal within the brain. Since DMG cells also frequently express EphA2 and IL13Rα2, the redesigned system could potentially target this childhood cancer without depending on a mutation present in only a subset of tumors.

To investigate the treatment, UCSF postdoctoral researcher Senthilnath Lakshmanachetty, PhD, administered B-SYNC CAR-T cells intravenously (IV) to mice implanted with human DMG cells. Some of the engineered cells entered the brain, activated their receptors, and attacked the tumors.

Tests showed that B-SYNC cells circulating elsewhere, including in the blood and spleen, did not produce the cancer-targeting receptors. This confirmed that their activation was restricted to the intended tissue, “just as we designed it,” Lakshmanachetty said.

The researchers next delivered the cells directly into the brain’s fluid-filled ventricles through an intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection. This method produced stronger results, completely clearing tumors in every treated mouse across two human DMG models. Conventional CAR-T cells, tested for comparison, again failed to control the cancer.

The scientists also investigated whether the modified immune cells could remain functional after the original tumors disappeared. Nearly seven weeks after treatment, they introduced another round of DMG cells into the mice. Every animal previously treated with B-SYNC rejected the new cancer cells.

One possible explanation involves T cell exhaustion, a condition in which prolonged stimulation gradually weakens the ability of immune cells to function. By restricting CAR production to the brain, B-SYNC may prevent the cells from becoming exhausted before reaching their targets. The researchers have not yet established whether this mechanism accounts for the treatment’s improved performance.

“We didn’t expect B-SYNC CAR-T cells to necessarily persist,” Lakshmanachetty said. “But they are still patrolling for cancer over 70 days out — and they’re still very functional.”

Following these laboratory results, the UCSF team is working with clinical oncologists to bring B-SYNC into human trials at UCSF Health. The first study, potentially beginning in April 2027, will evaluate the therapy in children and young adults with brain tumors. Each patient’s own T cells will be genetically modified to produce the B-SYNC treatment.

The trial, led by Marie Jaeger-Krause, MD, and Sabine Mueller, MD, PhD, will investigate different combinations of intravenous and intracerebroventricular delivery. For direct administration into the brain ventricles, patients will receive an implanted shunt connected to a reservoir beneath the scalp, allowing repeated treatments.

Although the mouse experiments demonstrated complete tumor clearance and durable protection, researchers still need to establish whether B-SYNC is safe and effective in humans.

“Diffuse midline glioma is a heartbreaking diagnosis for patients and their families,” said Mueller, director of the UCSF Pediatric Brain Tumor Center and co-founder of the Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium (PNOC). “This preclinical data is very promising. Mice with DMG are being cured, and we are incredibly excited to bring this therapy to the children and young adults we care for. This is exactly the kind of innovative approach they deserve.”

Reference: “Brain-sensing synNotch–CAR T cells enable precise targeting and clearance of diffuse midline glioma in multiple preclinical models” by Senthilnath Lakshmanachetty, Milos S. #6459. Scientists Discover a Mysterious Comet 808 Million Miles From Earth

A distant comet following a millennia-long orbit could provide valuable insights into how future space missions identify and study these elusive objects.

A space telescope built to study distant galaxies has discovered a previously unknown comet approximately 1.3 billion kilometers (808 million miles) from Earth. The European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope captured the object in images taken between September 16 and 24, 2026, marking its first discovery of a new comet.

Now designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid), the comet follows an orbit that takes thousands of years to complete. Rather than traveling close to the plane where the planets orbit the Sun, it is currently positioned far above that plane, as viewed from the Sun. Its distance from Earth is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point between Jupiter and Saturn.

Euclid was designed to map distant galaxies, not track comets and asteroids. Its observing strategy deliberately avoids the dust-rich band of sky along the Solar System’s plane, where scattered sunlight could interfere with sensitive measurements. The telescope also uses a “step-and-stare” approach that generally images each region only once, limiting opportunities to track moving objects over time.

Despite these obstacles, University of Helsinki researcher Mikko Pöntinen detected the comet using software he developed to identify moving Solar System objects in Euclid’s images. Working with the Euclid Consortium’s Solar System Objects Science Working Group, he found evidence of the object in five separate image sets.

“I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position, I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets [4]. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.”

The fuzzy cloud surrounding the object was a sign of cometary activity. As ice in a comet warms and releases gas, it can carry dust into space, forming a diffuse envelope known as a coma. This distinguishes active comets from most asteroids, which typically lack such visible clouds.

After finding no matching object in existing comet and asteroid catalogs, Pöntinen reported the observations to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC). The report prompted follow-up observations by ground-based astronomers, and the MPC officially confirmed the discovery on October 8, 2026.

“Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet’s orbit and Euclid’s scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images,” said Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist and a member of the discovery team.

Identifying moving objects is necessary for Euclid’s primary science mission because comet trails and other unwanted light can interfere with precise measurements of distant galaxies. The same detection techniques could also help astronomers discover comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun.

The rapid identification and confirmation of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) provides a practical test of how such discoveries could support ESA’s future Comet Interceptor mission. Although this particular comet is not a suitable target, the process demonstrates how Euclid’s observations could help scientists identify and assess other candidates.

“While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are, of course, happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on,” said Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

Archaeologists found several ancient weapons, intact vases and a bronze razor in the volcanic crater lake.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The 3,300-year-old weapon may have been deposited in the lake as an offering to a deity or for a high-status warrior who lived long before the rise of the Etruscans or the Romans.

The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome, according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years.

Bronze Age people erected pile dwellings or stilt houses in what is now Lake Mezzano, and archaeologists recovered parts of the submerged settlement during their recent investigations. According to the statement, researchers also found numerous intact vases, axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a bronze razor.

The bronze sword dates to the Late Bronze Age and may have been a symbol of power.

The sword and the razor were found near each other, suggesting the two artifacts may have been linked to a person of high social status, such as an elite warrior. But the placement of the metal weapons in a lake may also be related to a wider Bronze Age ritual practice where hoards of jewelry and bent or ritually "killed" artifacts were tossed into bodies of water. This practice continued through the centuries into Etruscan times, when wells were ritually "closed" with artifacts and human sacrifices.

During the 13th century B.C., people in central Italy engaged in trade networks that spanned the Mediterranean. "In this context, bronze weapons were not only instruments of combat, but also symbols of prestige, identity, and power," according to the statement.

The sword and other artifacts discovered in Lake Mezzano are giving archaeologists new information about the people who flourished in prehistoric Italy long before the Romans and Etruscans. Additional research is planned in the coming years, according to the statement.

#6456. Revolutionary Technology Could Transform How We Extract Lithium

A new breakthrough in lithium separation could help overcome major challenges in extracting this essential battery material.

A new technology developed at The University of Texas at Austin could make lithium extraction faster and more environmentally friendly by separating the valuable element from other dissolved substances with exceptional precision. The approach uses artificial channels so small they operate at the nanoscale, allowing lithium ions to pass through while blocking many competing ions.

Inspired by the molecular gateways found in living cells, the channels demonstrated two to five times greater lithium selectivity than other recently developed lithium transporters. Researchers report that the structures rank among the most selective lithium channels created to date, offering a potential alternative to conventional extraction methods.

Lithium is essential for batteries used in smartphones, electric vehicles, and electrical grids. It occurs in underground saltwater deposits known as brines, hard rock formations, and used batteries. However, these sources also contain elements such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium, whose ions can be difficult to separate from lithium. Existing extraction techniques often require considerable time and energy and can generate harmful waste.

“Lithium is in our phones, our cars and the power grid, but getting it out of the ground cleanly is still a hard problem,” said Manish Kumar, a professor in the Fariborz Maseeh Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering and the McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering who is one of the leaders of the new research published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. “Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner and easier to run.”

The researchers designed tiny pores within membranes that mimic the selective transport pathways of biological cells. Their ability to distinguish lithium from other ions depends on two features working together: chemical groups positioned at the channel entrance and the tightly confined space inside. Interactions at the entrance, combined with the channel’s internal structure, favor lithium transport while restricting competing ions.

The study builds on earlier research into separating rare earth elements, which are important for technologies including wind turbine magnets and electronic displays. By extending the underlying design principles to lithium, the researchers are developing a broader approach to selectively recovering critical minerals.

“We now have a toolkit rather than a one-off result,” said Harekrushna Behera, a research scientist in Kumar’s lab. “By understanding how ions interact with the chemical groups at the channel entrance, we can work toward designing more selective channels for lithium and potentially other critical minerals.”

The next challenge is incorporating these highly selective channels into membranes large enough for practical lithium recovery. The team is exploring a recently developed material made from interconnected, cell-like layers that can be constructed using lipids or plastic-like polymers. Such membranes could eventually support continuous lithium separation without harsh chemical solvents.

Although the laboratory results demonstrate strong selectivity, the technology has not yet been validated for industrial extraction. Researchers still need to test its performance using real brines, where numerous dissolved salts coexist, and determine whether the channels can maintain their effectiveness at larger scales.

Beyond recovering lithium from natural deposits, the researchers envision using the same technology to reclaim the element from discarded batteries. Another possible application is improving the separators inside batteries themselves, although further development will be needed to establish whether these uses are practical.

Reference: “Highly Selective Artificial Lithium Channels” by Harekrushna Behera, Tyler J. Duncan, Laxmicharan Samineni, Hyeonji Oh, Chenhao Yao, Raman Dhiman, Siqi Wang, Luke Hatch, Venkat Ganesan and Manish Kumar, 24 October 2026, Journal of the American Chemical Society. DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c13878

#6455. A Rare Radioactive Element Reveals a Hidden Secret About the Heaviest Atoms

Using advanced laser spectroscopy on extremely rare radioactive material, researchers have uncovered new insights into the structure of heavy atomic nuclei.

The nucleus of fermium-255 is far from spherical. Scientists have now determined its shape for the first time, finding that it is strongly elongated, much like a rugby ball. The high-precision measurements, published in Physical Review Letters, also correct earlier nuclear data and provide new evidence supporting theoretical models of the heaviest elements.

Fermium-255 contains 100 protons and 155 neutrons. In such heavy nuclei, the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons creates conditions that can lead to spontaneous fission, in which a nucleus splits into smaller fragments. Nuclear shape influences this process, making it a critical factor in predicting whether even heavier, potentially longer-lived elements can exist.

Rather than observing the nucleus directly, researchers studied its interactions with the electrons surrounding it. Electrons close to the nucleus are sensitive to its size, shape, and magnetic properties. These interactions produce extremely small differences in atomic energy levels that can be detected through precise laser measurements.

This phenomenon, known as hyperfine interaction, arises from the electromagnetic properties of the nucleus. A deformed nucleus interacts with the electric field of nearby electrons, while nuclear magnetism produces additional effects. Because fermium-255 has an odd number of neutrons, its nucleus also possesses a magnetic moment that contributes to the splitting of electronic energy levels.

Scientists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) first observed atomic energy levels in fermium more than 20 years ago. However, the technology available then could not resolve the fine details needed to determine its nuclear structure accurately. Some of the resulting nuclear data remained incomplete or inconsistent.

Fermium must be manufactured artificially, and obtaining enough atoms for an experiment requires an unusually complex production process. The researchers began with months of neutron irradiation of transuranium material at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA), producing einsteinium-254.

After initial experiments in the United States, the material traveled to Mainz (Germany) for processing and then to the Institute Laue-Langevin in France for additional neutron irradiation. This produced einsteinium-255, which decays into fermium-255. The material was subsequently returned to Mainz for spectroscopy experiments.

Einsteinium-255 has a half-life of approximately 40 days, allowing it to supply fermium-255 over several weeks. Through repeated chemical separations, scientists obtained individual samples containing tens of millions to about one billion fermium atoms. At JGU’s RISIKO separator, the samples were heated to approximately 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit) to release atoms for laser analysis. Specialized Ti laser systems excited and ionized the atoms, enabling researchers to resolve the hyperfine structure of two optical transitions despite the extremely small quantities available.

Researchers combined the experimental spectra with advanced atomic calculations performed at Jagiellonian University in Kraków, Poland, and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz (HIM). The analysis confirmed that the fermium-255 nucleus has a strongly prolate shape, meaning it is stretched along one axis. It also produced a magnetic dipole moment that differs from previously tabulated values, correcting earlier results that were inconsistent with physical expectations.

The measurements agree closely with modern nuclear theories developed by research groups in France and Germany. By providing more reliable information about nuclear deformation and magnetism, the findings strengthen models of nuclear fission and could improve predictions of the stability of superheavy elements that have yet to be discovered.

Reference: “High-Resolution Laser Spectroscopy on the Hyperfine Structure of Fm255 (Z=100)” by Mitzi Urquiza-González, Matou Stemmler, Thomas E. Colorectal cancer in young people shows genetic and structural differences that may make it more aggressive and treatment-resistant than the cancer tends to be in older people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why.

A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients.

The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson, a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital.

"I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers."

Many questions surround early-onset colorectal cancer, as the disease is rising in people under 50 even as it falls in older populations. It's now the leading cause of cancer death in the U.S. for people under 50, and its numbers are even on the rise among children and adolescents.

Beyond questions about what's driving this uptick in cases, another mystery has been why this disease is so deadly in young people.

"The clinical data suggests that the disease in the younger patients is more aggressive overall," Anderson said. "The patients, being very healthy otherwise, do not do well with treatment."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The reason why colorectal cancer is often aggressive in younger patients hasn't been clear.

To investigate that mystery, Anderson collaborated with Dr. Kimmie Ng, an oncologist at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Dr. Ramnik Xavier, a gastroenterologist at the Broad Institute and Mass General Brigham. They used a method of analyzing RNA in cells that allowed them to work with frozen and banked tumor tissue. RNA, a cousin of DNA, reflects the genes that are active in cells. In all, the team analyzed 189 tumors: 54 from patients under 50 and 135 from patients over 50.

With that many samples, the researchers could look at gradual differences tied to each age group, instead of just comparing tumors between the younger and older groups overall. That enabled them to pinpoint subtle differences, Anderson said.

For starters, younger people had a higher proportion of connective tissue cells in their tumors than they did of malignant cancer cells. That pattern was flipped in patients of older ages. Having a smaller proportion of malignant cells might sound good, but connective tissue in tumors can secrete compounds that suppress the immune system, Anderson said. That helps protect the tumor from immune cells that might otherwise target its cells for destruction.

These connective tissue cells can also physically block chemotherapy drugs from getting to the cancerous cells. This could be one reason younger patients' cancers resist treatment, the researchers suggested.

Based on patterns of gene activity in the tumors, the researchers suspect that younger patients' cancer cells also show distinct activity related to cell-to-cell communication. That may help the cells migrate through the body more easily than cancer cells in older patients do. In other cancers, this kind of gene activity has been linked to more aggressive tumors and a greater chance that the disease will spread, or metastasize, Anderson said.

The study's results also turned up an intriguing mystery: the presence of lots of long noncoding RNA. These strands of RNA contain more than 200 building blocks, called nucleotides, that don't provide instructions for building proteins. Coding RNA, in contrast, is ferried to protein-building factories in cells to be used as blueprints.

Scientists don't know what much of this long noncoding RNA does in the body, nor do they understand what it is doing in the tumors specifically. However, they hope to find out.

Anderson and her team are already working on manipulating the RNA they found inside cancer cells in petri dishes. In time, this line of research could supply another piece of the puzzle, helping scientists understand why colorectal cancer is so aggressive in young people.

"It's a new avenue for research into this disease that we previously had no idea about," Anderson said.
