#6452. A Hidden Weakness in the Brain’s Defenses Could Help Explain Alzheimer’s Disease

A protein buildup damaged the brain’s protective barrier in animal experiments, pointing to a possible target for Alzheimer’s treatment.

Roughly one in five people carries at least one copy of APOE ε4, the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. Yet many people with the variant remain mentally sharp into their 80s without developing the disease. Understanding what protects some of them could help researchers find ways to protect others.

APOE ε4 carriers accumulate unusually high levels of a protein called fibronectin at the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed layer of cells around brain blood vessels that helps remove toxic substances. Two years ago, Columbia University researchers discovered that a rare mutation in FN1, the gene that encodes fibronectin, limits this buildup and its damage, helping protect some carriers against Alzheimer’s. A drug that mimics that effect might offer similar protection.

The team’s latest study, published in Nature Aging, found that excess fibronectin can make the barrier leak in animal experiments and traced the damage to disrupted signals between cells.

“This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism,” says Caghan Kizil, the study’s corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer’s Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

“We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer’s, but we didn’t know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism—and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection.”

In human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, high fibronectin levels were associated with inflamed astrocytes. These cells, also called astroglia, help maintain the blood-brain barrier. Genetic and epigenetic analyses, which examined genetic variation and gene regulation, also linked FN1 to vascular disease and changes in VEGFA, a growth factor needed to maintain healthy brain blood vessels.

“The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process,” says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on the discovery of the protective FN1 mutation.

To investigate how fibronectin affects the barrier, the researchers also used human stem-cell models, three-dimensional vascular cultures, and experiments in zebrafish and mice. Their methods included single-cell sequencing and spatial imaging. Across the systems they examined, the findings pointed to APOE ε4 increasing fibronectin and promoting its accumulation around brain blood vessels.

In mice carrying human APOE ε4, brain fibronectin levels were nearly twice those in mice carrying the normal human APOE version, APOE ε3. The higher levels coincided with evidence that the blood-brain barrier was leaking. That comparison alone could not establish whether fibronectin caused the damage, so the researchers performed a more targeted test. They increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes to determine whether excess protein in those cells was enough, by itself, to compromise the barrier.

“The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association,” says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved.”

The researchers traced the damage to disrupted communication between cells. Excess fibronectin sends abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that sense a cell’s surroundings, and an enzyme called focal adhesion kinase. This disrupts a chain of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. These factors allow astrocytes and blood-vessel cells to communicate and work together to maintain the barrier.

“Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain’s blood vessels,” says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer’s tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling.”

The human findings suggest that the same damaging processes likely occur in Alzheimer’s patients who carry APOE ε4, although the evidence that excess fibronectin itself can cause barrier leakage came from the animal experiments.

The findings suggest three possible treatment strategies for people with APOE ε4. Researchers could try to prevent excess fibronectin from accumulating, block the harmful signals it triggers, or restore the growth signals needed to keep the blood-brain barrier healthy. The team is exploring these possibilities in laboratory experiments.

Any future treatment would need to target pathological fibronectin while preserving its normal roles in tissue structure and repair. Understanding the mechanism provides a foundation for developing more selective interventions and determining when they might be most useful.

“By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working,” says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. “Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s to an early disease process that may be possible to modify.”

#6451. The human voice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Our voices have superpowers. From a coach firing up a soccer team before a big game to a mother soothing a cranky baby in the middle of the night, the human voice is key to expressing feelings and forging connections. The tone of a person’s voice might even communicate feelings to loved ones better than facial expressions. So what happens to a person when their voice disappears?

People who have lost the ability to speak due to neurodegenerative disease or brain injury are talking again thanks to groundbreaking technologies that can decode the instructions the brain sends to speech muscles. For this issue’s cover story, senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders interviewed Casey Harrell, a man who regained his voice — lost to ALS — through a brain-computer interface.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

You can listen to Harrell in his own words in Season Two of The Deep End, our award-winning podcast. Harrell told Sanders: “It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”

In the podcast, Sanders digs into other innovations, including AI voice cloning, as well as the sinister potential of such technology to hijack people’s voices. “It might be used in a way people don’t want to have happen,” she says. Hear more wherever you get your podcasts.

In this issue, we also report on the progress in developing an effective treatment for stiff person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disorder that makes the body’s muscles freeze without warning. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration hasn’t yet approved any treatments for the disorder, which occurs in roughly 2 in 100,000 people. But that could some day change. Researchers are testing new CAR T cell therapies, senior writer Meghan Rosen reports. The process involves modifying a patient’s white blood cells so they wipe out harmful immune cells. Scientists hope a single treatment could cure the disease.

And there’s more controversy about using AI in mathematics, senior physics writer Emily Conover reports. OpenAI made waves when the company announced that it had solved one of the most famous puzzles in math — a day after mathematicians reported advances on a similar problem. The development is among a flood of AI-fueled achievements this year and raises big questions about who gets credit when the algorithms are doing the work.

A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.

This section of the Lumina simulation shows the gas temperature in different parts of the early universe, with redder areas showing active galaxy clusters.

In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.

The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.

"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.

Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.

The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Zier, O., Smith, A., Shen, X., Liu, R., Kannan, R., Koehler, S. M., Springel, V., Pakmor, R., Vogelsberger, M., Bulichi, T., & Hernquist, L. (2026). Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469

#6448. Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?

Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice.

The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal.

And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. Who approached whom? Were these interactions consensual? Were they the result of violence or trade alliances? Who raised these hybrid babies? And what does the genetic record tell us about the social lives of two different kinds of humans navigating each other's existence for the first time?

Some of the answers, it turns out, are written on the X chromosome — and they are stranger than expected.

The first high-coverage Neanderthal genome was sequenced in 2010, and for the next 15 years, researchers kept noticing something puzzling: Neanderthal DNA was less common from the X chromosomes in people alive today.

One of the two sex chromosomes in humans, the X chromosome represents about 5% of the DNA in cells. Most females carry a pair of X chromosomes in each cell, while most males have one X and one Y.

Everywhere else in our genome, traces of long-ago breeding between Neanderthals and modern humans showed up in roughly consistent proportions. But on the X chromosome, there was far less Neanderthal DNA.

In people today, the X chromosome (bottom right) has less Neanderthal DNA than the non-sex chromosomes do.

The leading explanation was negative selection — the idea that Neanderthal gene variants unique to the X chromosome were somehow incompatible with modern-human biology and had been gradually eliminated from the gene pool over thousands of generations. It was a reasonable hypothesis, given that incompatibilities elsewhere in the genome did lead to the weeding out of Neanderthal DNA on other chromosomes over time.

To understand why the negative selection explanation didn't explain the X chromosome data, however, it helps to know what different parts of the genome actually do. Some stretches of DNA are protein-coding regions; they contain the instructions for building proteins, the molecular machinery that does most of the work inside cells. Others are regulatory sequences that don't build proteins themselves but help control when and how much of a protein gets produced. And then there are still other stretches of DNA that don’t appear to code for proteins or directly regulate gene expression, though researchers suspect at least some have functions we don’t yet fully understand.

Alexander Platt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, hypothesized that if the problem was that Neanderthal gene variants on the X chromosome were inherently harmful, modern-human X gene variants would have been advantageous in Neanderthals. As a result, X chromosomal DNA extracted from Neanderthal skeletons should show an excess of modern-human DNA in stretches of the genome where they'd provide measurable benefit. They reasoned that this excess would likely appear in protein-coding genes or the regulatory regions that control their expression, not noncoding DNA.

But that's not what they found. Instead, Neanderthal X chromosomes carried more modern-human DNA in the noncoding regions of the genome than in coding regions. This pattern didn't reflect selection for better gene variants. It was a signature of reproduction ‪—‬ a record of who was passing chromosomes to whom.

In a typical pregnancy, the mother contributes an X chromosome via the egg, and the father contributes either an X or a Y via the sperm cell. So, while an individual is guaranteed to inherit their mother's X, they don't necessarily carry their father's — males exclusively inherit their mother's X. That pattern differs from the other 22 pairs of chromosomes, which mothers and fathers contribute to equally. Across a population, then, two-thirds of X chromosomes are inherited from mothers and one-third from fathers.

This fact makes the X chromosome a particularly sensitive recorder of who was reproducing with whom.

Tracking the flow of X chromosomes can reveal trends in Neanderthal-human mating. If Neanderthal males paired with modern-human females more often than Neanderthal females paired with modern-human males, you'd see more modern-human X chromosomes flow into the Neanderthal gene pool.

X data suggests that when the two types of humans mated, the mother was usually a Homo sapiens.

When the team ran simulations to explore this idea, the data suggested what Platt described as a persistent, recurring mating preference: Males with more Neanderthal ancestry tended to reproduce with females with more modern-human ancestry. And this trend held across at least two distinct mating periods separated by around 200,000 years, said Platt.

This finding gave the researchers a new window into the timeline of mating between Neanderthals and modern humans. Platt's team identified at least two distinct pulses: one roughly 45,000 years ago, which produced the majority the Neanderthal DNA that lives on in non-African genomes today, and an earlier period over 200,000 years ago, whose genetic traces survived not in modern-human populations but in Neanderthals.

The pattern of Neanderthal males having offspring with H. sapiens females appears in both periods, separated by more than 150,000 years.

What the X chromosome data alone cannot say is why the pattern exists. It documents who reproduced with whom. It says nothing about who wanted whom.

That distinction matters, because the same genetic signature can emerge from very different causes, and some have nothing to do with sexual preference.

Rajiv McCoy, a geneticist at Johns Hopkins University, pointed out that biology alone could produce a genetic signal like this one. When closely related species interbreed, the success of a pregnancy can depend not just on whose genes are inherited but on which parent belongs to which group.

Even if Neanderthal genes work fine in a modern-human genetic background, hybrid pregnancies may simply have been more likely to succeed when the Neanderthal was the father rather than the mother. That's not because of either parent's sexual preferences, but because of how their respective biologies interacted in the womb, McCoy told Live Science.

Researchers have recently proposed a few mechanisms that fit neatly with this theory. One study suggests that Neanderthal red blood cells restricted fetuses' growth in the womb. Another proposed that Neanderthal mothers carrying hybrid offspring may have been more prone to preeclampsia, a life-threatening pregnancy complication. Nothing in the existing data definitively rules such causes, McCoy said.

Neanderthal males were more likely to produce hybrid offspring that contributed to our gene pool than were Neanderthal females.

In practice, the two explanations are hard to separate. "Our models have no way of distinguishing mating from mating that produces a viable and fertile offspring," McCoy said. If hybrid pregnancies failed more often when the mother was Neanderthal, the genetic record would look similar to a world where Neanderthal females mated less often with H. sapiens males. Sexual encounters that didn't result in offspring left no genetic trace.

For now, the question of what drove that bias — social preference, or biology — remains open. Whatever barriers existed between the groups, they clearly weren't absolute. Multiple distinct episodes of interbreeding over thousands of years, McCoy noted, is itself evidence that the fertility of hybrid individuals was "sufficiently intact to leave a lasting mark."

Bridget Alex, a researcher in human evolutionary biology at Harvard University who has spent her career reconstructing the timing and geography of Neanderthal-H. sapiens overlap, cautioned that all this is hampered by one fact: no direct archaeological evidence reveals how the two groups interacted.

"Despite a century and a half of Neanderthal research," she told Live Science, "no one's ever found a Neanderthal and Homo sapiens fossil in the same exact layer dated to the same exact period at the same exact site."

Instead, we have a regional and variable patchwork shaped by conditions that shifted over thousands of years and hundreds to thousands of miles.

Neanderthals inhabited a territory stretching from Siberia to Iberia to Southwest Asia between roughly 250,000 and 40,000 years ago. Modern humans were evolving in Africa during much of that span and came out repeatedly, in multiple waves, meeting Neanderthals in different times and places, with likely very different outcomes each time, Alex said.

"It's not like the Neanderthals living in what's now Spain could call up the ones in what's now Uzbekistan and be like, 'OK, what's our policy with modern humans? Do we kill them, have sex with them, ignore them?'" she said. "My assumption has always been that interactions would vary across time and space depending on the particular environmental conditions, social conditions, and just the whims of a particular group."

Grotte Mandrine contains artifacts from tens of thousands of years of Neanderthal occupation — and a single layer suggestive of Homo sapiens occupation.

At Grotte Mandrin, a cave in the Rhône Valley in southern France, archaeologists found one of the most illuminating records of what those encounters may have looked like. Ludovic Slimak, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toulouse who has spent years excavating the site, described it as something genetics alone can't offer: "an extraordinarily precise archaeological sequence of Neanderthals and [Homo] sapiens occupying exactly the same place," he told Live Science in an email.

Neanderthal artifacts fill layer after layer of radiocarbon and luminescence dating up to about 57,000 years ago. And then, in one thin layer dated to between 56,800 and 51,700 years ago, there's a set of different stone tools and a single tooth that appear to belong to H. sapiens. Then, in layers immediately above, beginning around 51,700 years ago, Neanderthal artifacts appear again. That group of modern humans arrived, lived briefly in a continent otherwise inhabited entirely by Neanderthals, and then disappeared.

"What strikes me most is not mixture but proximity without fusion," Slimak told Live Science in an email. In other words, the two groups left no trace of cultural exchange or shared practice.There were "two human populations occupying the same landscape, probably encountering one another, while remaining culturally and biologically very different," Slimak said.

Genetics also paints a portrait of two very different social architectures. Two sites exemplify the trends: At Sunghir, a burial site in Russia dating to around 34,000 years ago, two H. sapiens adolescents were interred head to head beneath thousands of ivory beads and mammoth-bone spears. Ancient DNA analysis showed they were not immediate family members, yet they were buried together in an elaborate ceremony that implies a social world much wider than their immediate group.

Graves from more than 30,000 years ago in Sunghir in Russia show that two adolescents buried together were not closely related, suggesting Homo sapiens had wider and more flexible social networks than Neanderthals.

In contrast, at Chagyrskaya, a cave site in Siberia, Neanderthals buried in what appears to be a single community layer included a father and his teenage daughter, and a second pair of individuals who shared roughly a quarter of their DNA.

While these are just two sites, they reflect a broader trend that shows up repeatedly in genetic data: Human groups tended to operate through what Alex described as a nested structure: Tens of thousands of years ago, small groups of perhaps 20 or 30 individuals maintained broader ties through ceremonies, intermarriage between human groups and exchange with other groups.

In contrast, data from Neanderthal sites reveal that they tended to cluster in small, tightly knit groups that remained relatively separate from other Neanderthal populations.

Homozygosity, or DNA regions where a person inherited two copies of the same gene variant, is an inverse measure of genetic diversity. Adapted from Skov et al, 2022.

Unlike modern humans, Neanderthals didn't regularly mate with individuals in other communities, Alex said. The result, written in their genomes, is that individuals within a single Neanderthal group were often closely related. Their genomes show low genetic diversity across the board, — "kind of suggesting they're always a population on the verge," Alex said, "like an endangered species."

Still, there had to be some out-group mating. At sites where researchers have extracted genomes from several Neanderthal individuals, the pattern is consistent: Male Neanderthals were more closely related to each other than female Neanderthals were to each other. Females, by contrast, seemed more likely to have come from elsewhere. This is the signature of a "patrilocal" social structure in which males stay in their birth groups and females move between them.

Neanderthals' insularity sharpens a key question: If Neanderthal groups weren't regularly folding in Neanderthal females from distant communities, they would probably be even less likely to incorporate female H. sapiens. So how did modern-human women end up producing offspring with Neanderthal men at all?

Fernando Villanea, a population geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, thinks the question may be framed backward. The image of Neanderthal males raising hybrid children with modern-human females within Neanderthal communities, he argues, probably inverts what actually happened.

Something the genomes of late Neanderthals — those living toward the end of their long history in Eurasia — make clear is that they were roughly 10 times more inbred than the modern human ancestors who were then expanding out of Africa in large numbers, he noted. That level of inbreeding isn't usually a choice; it reflects how small and fragmented Neanderthal populations likely were.

We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals.

Archaeological and paleoclimatic data fill in the context: The ecosystems Neanderthals were best adapted to were shrinking as the planet entered a warmer, more humid period. Modern humans, who had evolved in hotter, wetter African environments, were simply better suited to Europe's new conditions, experts think.

The resulting numerical imbalance changes how scientists think about mating between Neanderthals and modern humans.

"We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals," Villanea told Live Science.

In the crucial period between roughly 50,000 and 44,000 years ago, when much of the interbreeding that left a trace in our DNA took place, Neanderthal DNA made up 5% of the modern human genome. Given how heavily humans outnumbered Neanderthals at the time, "that's a lot of matings occurring between the two." The most likely story, Villanea proposes, is "human groups absorbing surviving Neanderthal individuals and raising their children in a mostly human group."

His 2018 study in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution established that this happened across multiple distinct episodes — and the later ones are particularly telling. Some ancient H. sapiens genomes from Europe around 40,000 years ago, according to the study, carry Neanderthal ancestry from individuals who lived just a few generations after archaeologists can no longer find any physical trace of Neanderthals in the region at all.

Even the very last Neanderthal survivors were still contributing to the H. sapiens gene pool. A 2024 study by Leonardo Iasi and colleagues similarly determined that almost 90% of total Neanderthal ancestry in humans today came from a main pulse roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, likely in the Middle East, with the rest trickling in from more sporadic encounters scattered across Eurasia.

That paints a picture of meetings becoming rarer and rarer as Neanderthals disappeared, with hybridization continuing whenever they did meet up. "This, to me, says deliberate integration of Neanderthal individuals into human groups," Villanea said.

We know that some hybrid Neanderthal-H. sapiens survived because "we still carry the legacy of their existence," Alex said. However, we know they didn't thrive, because the Neanderthal ancestry of our ancestral populations eroded quickly.

While some hybrids survived, they likely suffered from health problems.

Most genes work in concert with other genes across the genome. When Neanderthal-specific variants entered the modern-human genome, it was like trying to put gears from one machine into a slightly different one; the parts didn't quite fit together. As a result, natural selection removed the Neanderthal variants rapidly. Villanea's calculations, based on the rate at which chromosomes recombine during cell division, suggest the drop from the original approximately 5% Neanderthal DNA roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago to the roughly 2% carried today happened in around 10 human generations.

"That's very fast," he said. "In real-life terms, that means a lot of hybrids did not survive to reproduce, and the ones that did probably had to deal with life-long health problems."

Platt's team looked at genetic evidence from multiple sites across Eurasia and found that the genetic purge ran in the opposite direction, too. Modern-human DNA was also being selected out of Neanderthal genomes.

Neither had inherently superior genes, Platt concluded. The gene variants were simply optimized for the separate evolutionary histories of their respective lineages, hundreds of thousands of years of independent adaptation that made certain combinations disadvantageous, if not fatal.

If Neanderthal males and modern-human females really were producing more surviving offspring than the reverse pairing, where did those children end up?

Villanea was cautious about reading too much into the X chromosome pattern on its own to answer that question. The imbalance Platt found is real, he said — not a statistical quirk. But "there is nothing in the X chromosome data that says it's based on human or Neanderthal mating preference," as Platt proposes.

The same pattern could, in theory, emerge from Neanderthal males leaving their birth groups to find mates, but as archaeological evidence suggests, this was not typical behavior. More likely, he argues, is something biological.

Hybrid children were likely raised in Homo sapiens groups.

In Peromyscus maniculatus and Peromyscus polionotus — two closely related species of North American deer mouse — a phenomenon called genomic imprinting causes hybrid offspring to develop differently in the womb depending on which species was the father and which was the mother. This pattern has nothing to do with behavior or preference. A similar process in early humans could have made Neanderthal father-H. sapiens mother pairings more likely to produce surviving offspring than the reverse, without either group consciously choosing anything.

"We simply don't know enough yet," Villanea said.

Distinguishing between these explanations — social behavior versus biological incompatibility — will require more Neanderthal genomes from the critical period of contact, ideally spanning multiple geographic regions, experts said.

There's another clue in genetic evidence from a 2026 study of 27 late Neanderthals who lived between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago in what is now Belgium and France. None of those individuals showed any sign of recent ancestry from modern humans, even as H. sapiens from the same era demonstrably carried Neanderthal DNA.

If hybrid children had been raised in Neanderthal groups and went on to reproduce there, those groups' genomes should retain traces of those events ‪—‬ but they don't.

As for whether modern-human groups were patrilocal — with males staying, females moving — the answer is considerably more variable than in Neanderthals. Modern-human communities across cultures show a range of patterns, with both sexes leaving their birth groups depending on circumstance, Alex said. That flexibility may have been part of what made human groups better able to absorb outside individuals.

Neither genetics nor archaeology has yet been able to answer the question at the center of this story: whether these encounters were by choice, by circumstance, or by force. Platt's team set it aside deliberately, and Alex is careful about it, too.

"We still wouldn't know if it was consensual or coerced," she said.

It's worth being specific about what different scenarios would look like archaeologically. If Neanderthal and modern-human individuals mingled through peaceful alliances, we might expect to find toolmaking techniques or symbolic objects crossing between groups at contact sites — precisely the kind of evidence that is absent at Grotte Mandrin, where, as Slimak noted, the two groups' technical traditions remained entirely distinct.

Slimak, writing from Grotte Mandrin in the middle of his excavation season, urged even more restraint. The genetic data, he said, are "consistent with an asymmetry" — gene flow moved more successfully through Neanderthal males and H. sapiens females than the reverse — but that is where the certainty ends.

The data says nothing about culture, desire, attraction or intent. "That entire social world has been added afterwards," he said.

The same signal, he pointed out, could emerge from a variety of histories — female mobility, demographic imbalance, alliance, exchange, capture, differential survival among hybrids. And these factors could contribute alone or in combination. Even the categories available for describing female movement may be too blunt. A single instance of migration, in traditional societies, can involve marriage, family strategy, alliance, obligation and violence all at once, in combinations that leave no trace for archaeology to disentangle.

"We may identify that a woman came from elsewhere," Slimak said. "We cannot recover her consent."

However, the convergence of genetics, demography and archaeology does reveal a structural picture, if not a sociological one.

The interbreeding was directional and repeated, patterned in ways that map onto the social organization of both groups — and driven in large part, Villanea's model suggests, by the sheer demographic weight of a growing human population folding in what remained of a disappearing one. Neanderthal males, in dwindling and insular communities, appear to have been the ones whose genes crossed into the larger H. sapiens world. Their children, in all likelihood, were raised as humans.

"Genes do not preserve past loves," Slimak said. "They preserve what was transmitted. And between transmission and lived experience lies almost the whole of human society."

#6446. Claude helped plan risky bird flu research. What did the AI add?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Anthropic’s Claude helped plan work with bird flu, but it’s unclear if harm was intended

H5N1 avian influenza virus particles (green) grow in kidney cells (purple). Anthropic’s Claude AI chatbot helped a scientist plan potentially risky bird flu experiments.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Anthropic’s Claude AI chatbot helped a scientist plan potentially risky bird flu experiments.

The researcher relied on Claude to plan studies, analyze data and choose experiments involving highly pathogenic avian influenza, the company reported September 10 in a threat intelligence report. The work sought to identify and introduce mutations that could help bird flu viruses adapt to mammals and transmit more easily between them. Anthropic says that, to its knowledge, no private company had previously publicly shared evidence of potential misuse of its platform for biological weapons development. But the company did not provide enough detail to determine whether Claude simply sped up work the researcher could already do or gave the researcher a new capability, experts say.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Learning how avian influenza viruses might pose a pandemic risk “is absolutely a normal part of virology research,” says influenza researcher Thomas Friedrich of the University of Wisconsin–Madison School of Veterinary Medicine. Such research can help scientists assess whether emerging bird flu viruses pose a greater risk to humans.

But experiments that deliberately aim to boost pathogen traits such as transmissibility or disease severity draw scrutiny, Friedrich says, because of concerns about accidents or misuse.

Though the report comes amid broader debates about the security of AI models, arguments over this “gain-of-function” research predate generative AI. In 2012, studies involving H5N1 bird flu and airborne transmission in ferrets prompted an international debate over whether the scientific benefits outweighed the risks. Some H5N1 transmission experiments were put on hold for a year while researchers and officials worked out how to handle the risks.In Anthropic’s case, discovered in May 2026, the bird flu researcher accessed Claude from a region where the service was not supported or available. Anthropic says the researcher used workarounds to access Claude anyway. Material shared with Claude suggested the group probably had physical access to relevant virus samples. Anthropic banned the researcher’s account in May for evading restrictions on access.Anthropic says it could not tell whether the researcher intended harm because legitimate and dangerous biological research can look similar. The company did not respond to questions from Science News about why it considered the case significant, how it assessed Claude’s role in the research or whether any proposed experiments had actually been performed.

Anthropic released too little information to determine the purpose of the work, says biodefense researcher Gregory Koblentz. “There is no evidence that any of this research was connected to the development of biological weapons,” says Koblentz of George Mason University in Fairfax, Va.

The same kind of biological research can serve very different purposes, from civilian science to military defense. Even work done at a military-affiliated institution does not, on its own, show that researchers are developing a biological weapon, Koblentz says.

Anthropic also did not provide enough detail to show exactly how much Claude helped, Friedrich says. The company’s own account suggests the AI model “did not meaningfully add scientific capability,” he says. In other words, it may simply have sped up the researcher’s work, rather than enabling something they could not have done otherwise.

Even if Claude’s role was only to speed up the work, that can make a big difference in a scientist’s workflow, says virologist David O’Connor of the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Systems such as Claude can help researchers find papers, synthesize results and parse data more quickly, he says. “Work or analyses that would have taken me months can now be done in an afternoon.”

As a result, existing scientific information, including about avian flu viruses, may become easier to find and use, O’Connor says. O’Connor says frontier AI models could let scientists tackle questions they might not have attempted before. “The frontier models will change the ambition of research questions that are asked,” he says.

The bird flu research was one of five instances in Anthropic’s report involving uses of Claude that the company says could support biological weapons development. None of the five look technically sophisticated or particularly concerning to biologist Kevin Esvelt of the MIT Media Lab. Esvelt is more suspicious of the researchers’ motives; he says the five cases showed signs of ill intent. But none “represented a competent attempt at weaponization.”

The poor quality of these particular attempts does not show what a more capable user might be able to do with AI-assisted biology, Esvelt says. AI can help with research and analysis, but turning an idea into a biological threat takes additional work, Koblentz says. “Even if AI is used to design a potentially dangerous pathogen, it is not a threat until the organism can be modified in a lab or synthesized.”

That requires facilities, measures for keeping viruses contained, funding, trained personnel and hands-on experience. Those barriers vary depending on who is doing the work, O’Connor says. They would be a major obstacle for an inexperienced person working alone, but less so for scientists with specialized training and access to a well-equipped laboratory.

Regardless, the remaining laboratory steps are substantial, Friedrich writes in an email. “There is a big gap between identifying mutations that could potentially adapt an avian influenza virus to humans and a ‘harmful biological outcome’.”

#6445. How to Survive the Zombie Apocalypse

The supplies you need to survive this (theoretical) disaster are probably already in your home.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Imagine this: You’re sitting at your dining room table, and the lights suddenly cut out. An alert buzzes on your phone—a mysterious infection is sweeping the nation. There’s a bang on the window behind you. You turn around to face a decaying figure, rotting fingers clawing at the glass pane. The zombie apocalypse just began. What are you going to do to survive?

While this scenario remains a feature of Halloween attractions, many of the same principles would apply in a true survival situation. In fact, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) even entertained a similar premise in 2011 with a comic aimed at teaching disaster preparedness. And, as it turns out, your home is already filled with ample supplies to survive this theoretical disaster—or, at the very least, challenge your DIY skills on an upcoming rainy weekend.

Perry Tancredi—deputy director at the Boulder Outdoor Survival School in Utah—explains in an email that, in any survival scenario, one poor decision can completely change the outcome of the situation. Because of this, it’s crucial to stay calm, Tancredi warns. He suggests popping a mint or candy in your mouth because the action should slow your mind during that initial adrenaline rush. (Tancredi recommends Altoids specifically, since their tin can also be useful in a disaster situation.) However, Tancredi jokes that this works better for slow zombies; the speedy variety might mean this tactic is the wrong decision, rather than what prevents you from making one.

Once you’ve settled your mind, survivalists tend to agree that shelter, water, and food should be your top priorities at the outset of any survival situation. Tancredi points to the rule of threes: “You can survive without food for about 3 weeks, without water for about 3 days, you can die of exposure (i.e. without shelter) in 3 hours, [and] an issue with your ABCs (airway, breath, and circulation) could kill you in about 3 minutes,” he writes.

Assuming that you can secure your house against any undead intruders, you should be able to quickly check shelter off the list of apocalyptic to-dos. Then comes water.

The CDC recommends emergency kits that have at least one gallon of water per person for each day. In a scenario such as a zombie apocalypse, meeting this quota is easier said than done, as water plants would likely shut down. Tancredi recommends filling up a bathtub at the beginning of an emergency for a passive water supply, especially if you’re boarding up your home.

If you do have outdoor mobility, Ricardo Castro, PhD—professor of materials science at Lehigh University in Pennsylvania—says there are already things in your house that could be used as a makeshift filter.

“I’d grab an empty plastic soda bottle, cut off the bottom, and turn it upside down like a funnel,” Castro says in an email. “I’d stuff some cotton or an old T-shirt into the neck, then add layers of washed sand, gravel, and small pebbles from the backyard. Pouring muddy water through these layers would remove much of the suspended dirt.” However, Castro notes that this wouldn’t actually purify the water, so boiling over something like a wood stove is still a crucial step to making your supply potable.

Finally comes food. Luckily, you likely already have many shelf-staples sitting in your pantry—canned goods are especially valuable, as the food is usually precooked during the packaging process. But this doesn’t mean you should let fresh produce go to waste, either.

You can harvest the seeds from common household ingredients, such as cucumbers and tomatoes, to raise in a hydroponic system. Ideally, this would allow you to run an at-home farm, without having to go outside and face the undead. While these setups can run up to a few thousand dollars in our current zombie-free world, some DIYers have also created their own with plastic storage bins and basic plumbing equipment—again, supplies you likely already have lying around your home.

Once your basic needs are settled, creating a power system may be advantageous for especially spooky nights. The internet is littered with these sorts of home-baked inventions, but a particularly promising gadget is a bicycle generator. (You can find PopMech’s instructions to make your own version here.)

This human-powered machine should generate enough power to run lights, charge phones, and power small appliances—and it’s made from supplies that are probably tucked away in your garage, shed, or forgotten corners of your basement. Perhaps the most exotic element needed is a 12-volt (or higher) DC motor, but never fear: These can be found anywhere from ceiling fans to small appliances to the automatic windows in your car.

There is an obvious drawback here: It takes a lot of human energy—or calories—to power this sort of machine. Castro suggests a DIY wind turbine as a passive power-generation method. He says he would start by taking apart a fan and searching for a motor, perhaps in a power tool or children’s toy. To capture enough wind, Castro says he might use scrap wood and fabric from bed sheets to fashion “something resembling an old Western windmill.” With the appropriate wiring, he says this could power LED lights or charge a small battery.

It’s also likely in your best interest to think about how to keep the zombies out—and let other humans in. After all, we’re a social species, and isolation can be detrimental if it goes on for too long, Tancredi notes. And it seems the solution here might be a simple one.

You’ll likely need fire for other purposes, such as purifying water and staying warm, but it could also serve as a way to scare off the zombies, Tancredi explains. For instance, we already see this in campfires deterring some wildlife. The smoke from the fire is also particularly useful, as it would let other survivors know you’re still out there, he adds.

While Tancredi’s defensive method might deter zombies from approaching, Castro’s offense would help drive away any undead visitors. Inspired by some of Leonardo da Vinci’s designs, Castro suggests assembling a “zombie ballista,” or a medieval military weapon used to launch objects, similar to a crossbow. Wooden furniture pieces and broomsticks could act as a main structure, and something like the rubber gasket on an old washing machine might work as a low-powered launcher, he says. Load objects from around your home into the machine and prepare to knock down any encroaching zombies.

By now, you have the toolkit to survive a zombie apocalypse—but luckily you won’t have to. Scientists suggest that this is, at the very least, an improbable scenario. For instance, the hit show The Last of Us featured mutated humans, hijacked by parasitic fungus. This sort of “zombification” is unlikely, as “the human brain is incredibly complicated for any organism to decipher,” Colorado State University entomologist Maia Holmes says in an article for the school.

But even if the zombie apocalypse isn’t a possibility—at least not within our lifetimes—entertaining it as a thought experiment certainly seems like a good way to flex your creative muscles and prepare for more realistic scenarios.

“The main message this exercise brings to me is that engineering becomes particularly valuable when conventional solutions are no longer available,” Castro writes. “We tend to think of engineering as requiring sophisticated equipment, but some of its most interesting applications come from understanding basic principles: mechanics, energy conversion, heat transfer, and filtration, and using whatever materials happen to be around us.”

Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other decapitated bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.

Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.

"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The facial reconstruction is based on the shape of the man's skull. He is shown here without a beard, which was based on what was common at this time.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Jess Turner, an osteoarchaeologist at National Museums Scotland, with the skull of the man buried outside the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.

The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.

What do you know about the Empire's conquest of the British Isles? Find out with our Roman Britain quiz!

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6443. I Can ‘Smell’ Thoughts. You Can Too—and It’s Secretly Shaping Your Life.

You may be able to sniff out everything from emotions to political beliefs.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Staring into the crowded refrigerator, I pushed containers of cold leftovers to and fro, willing a more appetizing late-night snack to appear. Over the low electric hum, I heard footsteps approaching from the other side of the open door. Before I saw my father’s somber face, a smell, or something like it, caught my attention. Instantly, I recognized it—not from the actual odor, as I couldn’t put my finger on any one recognizable scent, but more so from a memory.

This was the same way my dad smelled when he sat me and my sister down to tell us his own father had died. The same way he smelled when he picked me up early from high school to break the news about my maternal grandmother. The sadness in my dad’s voice came as no shock to me. Someone was dead. I knew with complete certainty that it was true. What I didn’t understand was how my nose knew it first.

Olfaction—or your sense of smell—is an integral part of human perception. It alerts us to potentially dangerous environmental factors such as smoke or gas, supports other senses such as taste, and a good sense of smell is even linked to lower rates of cognitive decline. Thinking back to that day in the kitchen, I began to wonder whether my sense of smell had tuned me into a silent conversation everyone else was missing. As it turns out, a growing volume of research suggests that scent is quietly shaping how we perceive one another and, more broadly, our reality. For some, it even appears to be a superpower—allowing them to detect, just through their sense of smell, illnesses and undiagnosed diseases in others.

One of these super smellers is a woman named Joy Milne, whose sense of smell is so acute that she’s able to detect when someone has tuberculosis, cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer’s disease, or Parkinson’s disease. Researchers put Milne’s nose to the test in a 2019 study published in ACS Central Science. The team asked two groups—one afflicted with Parkinson’s disease and the other healthy—to wear identical T-shirts overnight. When Milne smelled the shirts the next day, she was able to correctly sort all but one using just the power of her sniffer.

Months later, the participant whose smell Milne had mistakenly slotted into the Parkinson’s category reported that he had been diagnosed with the disease. Milne’s nose had picked up on something long before doctors had diagnosed it.

Pamela Dalton, PhD, MPH, studies the link between human olfaction and our cognitive and emotional processes at the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, a scientific institute researching taste and smell. She says that, while not everyone has a nose attuned to medical maladies, the human olfactory system is constantly working overtime to decode and process the world in much more subtle ways.

In fact, when I confessed the story about my father announcing that my great-uncle had died, Dalton wasn’t fazed.

Dalton says humans communicate their feelings to each other through chemical molecules released in sweat, tears, or breath. These are called emotional chemical signals or emotional chemosignals. When the signals you give off reach another person, their olfactory system detects and interprets the chemicals. However, these aren’t processed the same way as regular smells.

Most of the time, we connect our smells to other senses stored in our memories—how a food tastes, or how salty ocean air may feel calming. If you’re sitting in front of a slice of pizza, for example, those molecules bond with the sensory receptors in your nose, generating an electric current that ends up in two areas of your brain that are associated with your sense of smell—the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex. As the current continues traveling through your brain, regions associated with memory and emotional regulation complete higher processing to link that signal with your previously stored understanding of the smell of pizza.

With chemosignaling, on the other hand, a final association is never made. This is likely why the scent on my dad was familiar but not recognizable. In fact, to most people, chemosignals have no recognizable fragrance at all—so you won’t find a Yankee Candle that smells like sadness or an air freshener that reeks of stress.

Instead, chemosignaling acts as an invisible guiding force. It’s something most of us do all the time. We unconsciously filter our perception of people and the world around us through these involuntary olfactory noticings. These signals cause us to constantly make little judgments about others, everything from what someone’s feeling to whether they’d be a good romantic partner.

You May Be Able to Smell Political Beliefs

Opposite-party partnerships are uncommon, according to an ever-growing body of research. Researchers put that partisan divide to the test in a 2014 study published in the American Journal of Political Science where they tried to determine whether our sniffers play a role. The team found that participants were more attracted to the smell of people whose political beliefs aligned closely with their own. Crucially, the study subjects didn’t see the people whose scents they were analyzing, meaning visual attraction played no role in the end results.

Dalton says the process of sending and receiving chemosignals usually bypasses conscious thought, meaning that we do it involuntarily and without noticing it. “It’s not like we’re [observing these chemical signals] and going, ‘Oh… she’s sad, I’m smelling her sad odor,’” Dalton says.

However, that doesn’t mean that these signals go completely unnoticed. When your olfactory system senses someone else’s chemosignals, it can trigger changes in your perception, mood, or physical reaction, Dalton adds. In everyday terms, this may look like feeling inexplicably on edge around a friend who’s secretly stressed about a presentation they have at work the next day.

Nicholas A. Christakis, MD, PhD, MPH, is a social scientist at Yale University and the director of the school’s Human Nature Lab, a project dedicated to understanding human interaction. Christakis affirms Dalton’s ideas about chemosignals, pointing to something much deeper in our species’ history. He explains that humans evolved in a “very logical way,” since we emit volatile chemicals into the air during our most vulnerable, fear-filled moments. These chemicals then change the behavior of those around us in ways that, theoretically, would enhance survival, he says.

Christakis poses a few scenarios in which our ancestors might have felt danger, such as seeing a lion or a fire. “It’s not hard to imagine why, as a social animal, it would be useful to us to communicate to our brethren, ‘I'm afraid,’” he says. In terms of his analogy, if Christakis sees the lion and subconsciously emits these stress chemicals, you may realize he’s in trouble. “By signaling that I’m afraid, I might elicit from you some help,” he adds.

In a more modern example, Christakis points to the intoxicating aroma of a newborn baby. He says that a key part of this smell is an organic compound called hexadecanal. Hexadecanal is completely odorless, meaning that, if you smelled a sample on its own, your brain wouldn’t immediately conjure images of babies.

Despite this, a study published in Science Advances showed that participants unconsciously changed their behavior when asked to smell samples of hexadecanal. Specifically, men showed decreased aggression levels while women displayed the opposite. The theory, Christakis says, is that smelling a baby unconsciously causes people to become more nurturing and protective.

Unlike the participants in the study, I was more conscious of the odor that clung to my dad all those years ago. Still, Dalton explains that what I “smelled” most likely wasn’t the scent of death itself. My olfactory system responded with amplified alertness because it registered the release of chemical signals, perhaps those associated with stress, sadness, or anxiety. Simply put, I didn’t smell the future—I recognized an olfactory pattern I had previously encountered.

Dalton says it’s actually not that uncommon to become attuned to the chemical signals of people you spend a lot of time with. For instance, in a 2010 study published in Social Neuroscience, participants were able to detect heightened emotions in their romantic partners just by smelling their body odors. Additionally, people were more accurate when smelling their partner’s samples compared to those of strangers.

In fact, Dalton herself has even developed a keen nose after years of working with thousands of fear and anxiety sweat samples—a skill that she showed off on an episode of MythBusters. She notes that stress sweat has “a very different quality” than exercise sweat, though she avoids describing the scent to keep herself open to variations, since not everyone’s signals smell the same.

While Dalton acknowledges that there is still much to be learned in this field, she believes that these signals play a major role in shaping human interaction and perception. In short: It seems like sometimes you really should follow your nose.

#6442. Volcanoes lurk behind the scenes of human history

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cold spells after eruptions may have spurred famine, disease, revolt and religious changes

German artist Caspar David Friedrich painted Two Men by the Sea in 1817, two years after Mount Tambora’s eruption in present-day Indonesia. Though far away, the blast spread volcanic aerosols around the world and may have inspired the image’s dark sky.

Caspar David Friedrich (Wikimedia Commons)

“The bright sun was extinguish’d … and the icy earth swung blind and blackening in the moonless air.” These words from Lord Byron’s 1816 poem Darkness evoke a hellish apocalypse. But Byron may have been inspired by the fallout of a real cataclysm — one that happened half a world away.

Mount Tambora, in present-day Indonesia, blew its top in 1815. More than 71,000 people in the vicinity died. And climate-cooling aerosols from the eruption ushered in extreme weather the following years in far-flung places. Cold weather in the summer of 1816, sometimes with frosts and snow, destroyed corn in New England, rice and buckwheat in China and wheat, oats and potatoes in Ireland. In some places, the rising cost of bread sparked protests and riots. The circumstances may have helped spread typhus. Some called 1816 “the year without a summer,” others “the year of the beggars.”

Like Tambora, volcanoes, and the cooling they cause, may be an underappreciated geologic force at times moving behind the scenes of human history.

“These climatic impacts of the Tambora eruption were recorded without any knowledge that this had anything to do with an eruption,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge.

While Tambora is the most well-studied eruption in history, others have also rattled the planet. Oppenheimer and his colleagues analyzed 38 large eruptions in the 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Their work pulled together studies linking the geologic events and their effects on climate with their potential societal fallout in food systems, the economy, unrest, culture and religion. The locations and exact timing of the eruptions that spurred some notable cold spurts aren’t known. But understanding how the events impacted the climate, environment and society can offer clues to the past, including how people coped with climate stress.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Volcanic eruptions, they are kind of this like hammer blow to the climate system,” says Heli Huhtamaa, a climate and environmental historian at the University of Bern in Switzerland. Volcanoes may offer lessons about resilience for modern societies in a warming world, she says.

Volcanoes spew sulfur-containing gases. Over weeks, those gases react in the atmosphere to form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. Paintings from years after eruptions show bloodred sunsets or landscapes shrouded by hazy skies.

Because no two eruptions are exactly alike, it takes work to grasp each one’s impacts on weather and climate. “If we understand the climate response of one [eruption], that does not mean that we understand the climate response of another,” says Ulf Büntgen, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Cambridge.

A volcano’s explosivity impacts how high it shoots its gases and where they travel. Over time, those gases form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. In this computer model of a 1991 eruption, colors represent how high particles are in the atmosphere. Red is high and blue is closer to Earth’s surface.

Researchers find the traces of past eruptions in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists try to nail down the date on a sulfur-loaded ice core layer and compare it with tree ring data, a logbook of sorts for summer growing conditions since temperatures impact how trees lay down their wood each year. Scientists can pull together tree ring records from far-flung places and use statistics to work out annual temperatures in a hemisphere.

Cold spells sometimes jump out from tree ring records. For years when cool summers impeded the final stages of wood formation, a chemical method used to estimate temperatures turns wood layers blue. Büntgen and colleagues saw two blue rings around 1345. “And that is very rare. We never saw that two years in a row,” he says. The rings coincided with the timing of the Black Death’s spread in Europe, the team reported in 2025 in Communications Earth & Environment. The researchers traced the connections between chilly summers, poor grain harvests in the Mediterranean and shipping records showing how Italian city states imported flea-ridden grain from the Caucasus.

Oppenheimer, Büntgen and their colleagues broadened the detective work for their 2026 review. The team studied Northern Hemisphere temperature responses to the 38 largest eruptions between A.D. 1 and 1900. On average, each volcano caused about 0.5 degrees Celsius of cooling in the year after the eruption. Recovery to normal temperatures was slower for eruptions that occurred in times that were already colder on average, Büntgen says. In some periods, large or successive eruptions may lead to an elevated amounts of particles in the atmosphere for a long time. The team’s calculations show that high aerosol levels concur with some of the past two millennia’s coldest spells, such as the one preceding the Black Death.

Those cold snaps often had dire consequences. Out of 17 large-scale famines in Europe from 1300 to 1800, 11 followed major eruptions. In addition to faltering crops and famines, the most frequently societal responses described in studies collected by the review authors were disease outbreaks, political turmoil and migration.

The societal circumstances surrounding eruptions are as important as the amount of cooling, Huhtamaa says. She and her colleagues studied crop failures and farmstead desertion in three different volcanic eruptions that impacted Ostrobothnia, in what is now Finland. During the 17th century, Ostrobothnia experienced cooling from three sets of eruptions at different time periods.Although the latest eruption event, in 1695, was the coldest of all, peasants fared better than they had after eruptions earlier in the century, Huhtamaa and colleagues reported in 2022 in Climate of the Past. Though people still starved, only around 7 percent of peasants lost their farmland, compared with 20 percent in the other periods. This was because the crown provided tax relief, Huhtamaa says. This wasn’t humanitarian aid, as it was meant to preserve the tax base and prevent possibly decades of lost revenue.“When there is a climatic shock, it doesn’t matter if it’s 0.5 or 1.5 degrees cooler, because what really matters is the societal vulnerability,” Huhtamaa says.

Studies like Huhtamaa’s reveal how societies can tick on in spite of climate disasters. But historians haven’t always been keen to look to climate for clues to explain history. Human agency has often been considered the only reasonable explanation for human affairs, Huhtamaa says. “And climate explanations sounded lazy.”

Investigating societies’ preconditions and responses to the climate change caused by volcanoes could help people prepare for a now warming world. A recent report from the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, noted that not enough research had been done on responses, Huhtamaa says. Researchers could examine one place’s response to different events, as in Huhtamaa’s work on Ostrobothnia, or parse different locales’ responses to the same event. Meanwhile, greater use of insights from ecology, agronomy and economics, for instance, can help with this detective work that reveals how humans respond to climatic events beyond their control.

Those responses appear in religion, too. For instance, lines in the famed 10th century poem Vǫluspá seem to reference the 939 eruption of Iceland’s Eldgjá volcano, with high-flying flames and blackened sun beams. “It’s like an eyewitness description of a phenomenal lava flood,” Oppenheimer says. The poem foretells a fiery end to pagan gods, such as Odin, who are replaced by one god. Vǫluspá, which explained the eruption in terms of divine displeasure,may have contributed to the island’s Christianization around 1000, Oppenheimer and colleagues suggest.

Famines, riots, disease, migration. The widespread climatic effects of volcanoes across the ages may be subtler than the hellscapes conjured by poets but more tangible in the marks they’ve left on history.

A biology student found a Native American stone spearpoint when searching for shark teeth along the coast of Virginia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On the last day of an ecology field trip to Virginia's Eastern Shore, a biology undergraduate student discovered more than she expected. While searching for shark teeth, Brooklyn Rolph, a student at Mary Baldwin University in Virginia, stumbled upon a stone spearpoint estimated to be around 4,500 years old.

"Wow, this is so crazy," Rolph said in a statement. Already primed to look for pointy objects underwater, Rolph found a stone spear and immediately alerted the professors running the trip. "They were ecstatic," she recalled.

The stone artifact is about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long and, according to local archaeologists, a type known as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point. This kind of stone tool was made by Indigenous people across the East Coast of the U.S. from around 4,500 to 3,000 years ago. Sometimes called a "broadspear," the stone point also may have been used as a knife by prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the Late Archaic period.

The stone point is likely 3,000 to 4,500 years old.

The field trip was part of an ecology course led by Mary Baldwin University faculty members who had secured a permit from the state to explore the barrier islands off the Eastern Shore, the southern part of the Delmarva Peninsula that includes most of Delaware and parts of Virginia and Maryland.

Just after a lunch break on Sept. 21, the last day of the excursion that aimed to let students study plants and animals in the coastal ecosystem, Rolph set out to quickly explore a mound of shells on the island and noticed the spearpoint at the edge of an inlet. Her professors were blown away by the lucky discovery.

"The set of circumstances that came together that made this possible is quite unbelievable," Paul Callo, a biology professor at Mary Baldwin University who was co-leading the trip, said in the statement. "The tide was coming in, so the spear point was soon to be buried."

When Rolph showed Callo the artifact, he was "truly at a loss for words," he said. "It is certainly awe-inspiring to see and touch something that was made by human hands thousands of years ago."

The barrier island where Rolph found the stone point is part of a natural area owned by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, which means the artifact is now the property of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Archaeologists collected it from the Mary Baldwin group and have taken it to the Virginia Department of Historic Resources for further study.

Rolph was fine with not keeping the spearpoint. "That's how you get cursed!" she said.
