#6440. A Mysterious Statue Emerged on Easter Island. More Could Be Hiding Right Beneath It.

Three years after the discovery, archaeologists still can’t say how old it is—or whether there are more.

In February 2023, a moai was found lying face-up among reeds in a dried lakebed on Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island. The roughly five-foot statue was small by the island’s standards, but its location surprised archaeologists. It was the first moai reported in the lakebed inside Rano Raraku, the volcanic crater where islanders carved many of their statues.

“The statue was a completed one meant for an ahu platform,” Terry Hunt, an archaeologist and professor of anthropology at the University of Arizona, tells Popular Mechanics. An ahu is a ceremonial platform where moai are displayed. Hunt says this one was carved from the bedrock on the nearby crater walls, then brought to the place where it was discovered.

As reported in our earlier coverage, Hunt described the surprise to Good Morning America. “There have been no moai found in the dry bed or in what was previously a lake, so this is a first.”

The location wasn’t the only surprise. The statue’s small size led Hunt to suggest, in a 2023 University of Arizona account, that it was probably carved early in the period between Polynesian settlement around 1200 and European arrival in 1722—small moai could have been made later, he allowed, but the largest ones likely came after those first years. That possibility is what gives the find its weight: if other early, small statues lie beneath the lakebed, archaeologists could compare them with later moai and trace how the island’s carvers progressed from modest figures to giants. Yet more than three years after the discovery, no one knows how old this moai is or whether it has company. Hunt says there’s been no further investigation.

The small statue could tell a bigger story

In 2023, Hunt was considering ground-penetrating radar to look for buried moai or architecture, particularly in the lakebed. Today, he’s more confident about finding statues buried in quarry rubble than beneath the lakebed. “There are almost certainly statues buried in the rubble and back dirt from quarrying activities in Rano Raraku,” he says. “Perhaps there are others buried in the lakebed sediments.”

A group of statues beneath the lakebed would give researchers more than another addition to the inventory. If they turned out to be early, their appearance and locations could offer clues to how the islanders carved moai and what they were doing around the lake. “Buried statues could be associated with new radiocarbon dates and give us a better idea of the early quarrying activities,” Hunt says. He adds that the statues could reveal stylistic differences that developed over time.

The dates have changed the argument before

Hunt and his colleagues have already shown how much a date can change the story of Rapa Nui. Their research challenged the claim that islanders stopped building monuments after their society collapsed, before Europeans ever arrived.

A 2020 study in the Journal of Archaeological Science examined the chronology of ahu construction at eleven sites. The researchers pieced together radiocarbon dates and evidence from the platforms themselves, alongside accounts from European visitors. They found that islanders kept building and using the monuments for at least 150 years after 1600, when their society was supposedly already in collapse.

The 2020 research changed the account of how long monument-building continued. Early lakebed statues could help fill in the other end of that history, showing what people were carving as the tradition developed.

Finding those statues and studying them are two different problems. “However, excavations in the quarry would be highly unlikely given conservation issues and the islanders’ sentiments about the site,” Hunt says. A geophysical survey could map buried moai without disturbing the ground, but it can’t date them or reveal the carving details that would show how the tradition developed. For that, archaeologists would need to see the stone itself. Conservation pressures cut the other way, too: the Easter Island Statue Project’s discovery report called for stabilizing the newfound moai and protecting its fragile surface, and Hunt notes the soft volcanic tuff continues to erode. The result is a strange bind. A survey could show exactly where Rapa Nui's early history lies, while the most revealing evidence stays underground.

#6439. Four Decades Ago, Scientists Dropped Gophers Onto a Volcano. They Might Try It Again.

Scientists’ experiment on Mount St. Helens suggests rodents can deliver fungi that plants need, but the repair crew has an appetite.

In 1982, scientists brought a pocket gopher to Washington’s Mount St. Helens and put it inside a small enclosure around a plant growing on the Pumice Plain. Two years after the volcano’s infamous eruption, the plant had taken root among volcanic deposits. The gopher stayed for 24 hours before the researchers returned it home.

Michael Allen and his colleagues were testing whether gophers could carry fungi themselves, rather than simply uncovering fungi in buried soil. Allen describes experiments around two plants in different volcanic deposits. When the researchers returned the following year, both plants had mycorrhizal fungi, while nearby plants outside the enclosures showed no traces of them.

“We concluded that the gophers themselves transported these critical fungi, likely in their feces as they are known to feed on these fungi in their meadows,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

The experiment went viral after a 2024 paper in Frontiers in Microbiomes reported microbial differences associated with the old gopher enclosures. That paper dates the Pumice Plain experiment to 1982, rather than the 1983 date repeated in some coverage. The researchers sampled the soil in 2014, when the gopher had been gone for about 32 years.

Allen, a soil ecologist and distinguished professor emeritus at the University of California, Riverside, thinks the gophers give us something else to consider. When we plant a damaged landscape, how do the microbes those plants need get there? Could gophers do the job? If so, people planting a former mining or industrial site would have a reason to let gophers stay, even when they eat some of the seedlings.

Some native gophers survived the May 18, 1980, eruption by hiding underground, beneath the snow cover. Allen says the snow and soil protected them in patches of meadow and land that had been logged. Where the ash wasn’t too deep, the gophers dug their way out, bringing the old soil up with them. They also brought microbes with them, including mycorrhizal fungi, which help plant roots obtain nutrients and water in exchange for carbon.

But the Pumice Plain was buried under more than 20 meters of sterile volcanic ash and debris, far beyond any gopher’s reach. Allen wanted to know whether a gopher could carry fungi onto ground like that from somewhere else. That’s why his research team took a gopher from a nearby clearcut and put it in the enclosure on the Pumice Plain. The results of the experiment were clear. The plants inside the enclosures had mycorrhizal fungi, but nearby plants outside did not. Allen suspects the fungi arrived in the gopher's droppings, although the experiment didn’t show how.

Decades later, the landscape around the experimental site had changed considerably. Allen says plants, gophers, and fungi have spread across the Pumice Plain, beyond the original plot. The later study, led by mycologist Mia Maltz, found differences in the microbial communities associated with historic gopher enclosures and comparison plots. It also examined the lasting influence of forest conditions before the eruption.

That finding leaves plenty to investigate. A different assortment of microbes doesn’t automatically mean healthier soil or faster recovery. Allen says that analysis of the communities is continuing. He wants to know whether gophers could bring those helpful microbes to other places where people are trying to get plants growing again.

When the nearest healthy soil is too far away

Allen thinks the question could matter most where damaged ground lies far from surviving vegetation. If healthy soil and vegetation are close by, he told Pop Mech, microbes may find their way back on their own. But microbes struggle to return to places like industrial sites, where healthy soil is scarce, and Allen thinks those sites could be worth testing to see whether gophers can help.

Allen’s work extends beyond volcanoes: at a Wyoming strip mine, his team moved gophers and soil from a healthy ecosystem onto disturbed ground. He suspects gophers deliver a broader mix of microbes than commercial treatments do, though he calls that a question for further research. Success would depend on conditions, though. As David Lindenmayer, a conservation biologist at the Australian National University, notes, an introduced animal first needs a habitat, and Allen adds that gophers need enough food to get started. Timing matters too, because the soil microbes that survived the eruption, which Lindenmayer calls “biological legacies,” die off without host plants, so the longer a site waits, the fewer remain to help new roots take hold.

That requirement brings an awkward complication. A gopher could make a meal of the seedlings it was brought in to help. The animals “could well destroy the restoration effort if they ate the plants desired for restoration and did not eat undesirable plants,” Allen says.

Lindenmayer also cautions that returning an animal to a changed landscape can produce surprises, because it’s hard to know how a gopher will affect the plants and animals that have moved in since it disappeared. Researchers would need to track whether gophers deliver useful microbes, whether those benefits outweigh the damage the animals do, and how the approach compares with other ways of helping a site recover. Allen’s experiment gives them a place to start: in a single day on volcanic ground, a gopher carried fungi to plants. The question now is whether more plants would survive with a hungry gopher around than without one.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a tiny new world in the far reaches of our solar system, hidden beyond the orbit of Neptune — and it is among the largest and brightest objects ever discovered beyond Neptune.

If confirmed, the miniature world would increase the number of officially recognized solar system dwarf planets to six. Upper estimates of the object's size place it at more than half the diameter of Pluto, the largest known dwarf planet.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and member of the Rubin team who wrote the code that helped discover the prospective dwarf planet, said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

The potential dwarf planet, designated 2026 ED138, orbits the sun at roughly 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun. The potential new planetoid has been hiding behind galactic camouflage; with its orbit tilted at a 25-degree angle from the solar system plane, it's at just the right angle to get lost in the light from the inner Milky Way, the researchers said.

Many telescopes struggle to see past the millions of stars making up our galaxy's bulge. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, however, images the entire southern sky every few nights with the largest digital camera ever built, sending out millions of nightly alerts for every object that has changed brightness or position. This makes it exceptional at identifying anything that moves, from solar system objects to transient events like supernova explosions.

The observatory had only just begun its 10-year mission of scanning the sky in July, and ED138 stood out in the data.

Holman works on the software algorithms that process the extreme amounts of data the observatory collects. The code he developed with his colleague, Kevin Napier, compares billions of observations to determine which ones are detections of the same moving object. Running data from Rubin through the code revealed the unusually large object.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By looking at past data from Rubin and archival images from the Dark Energy Camera mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (both in Chile), the team was able to map out ED138's orbit over the past 10 years.

The Kuiper Belt is a region of the solar system beyond Neptune that is a wild frontier of small, mostly icy bodies made from frozen methane, ammonia, water and rock. It ranges from roughly 30 to 50 times the distance between Earth and the sun, and is home to most of the known dwarf planets, including Pluto. Thousands of Kuiper Belt objects have already been discovered. These space rocks can be frozen time capsules that hold clues about the early solar system's formation.

A model of the solar system showing the five dwarf planets officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) and the orbit of the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138.

Dwarf planets are the largest Kuiper Belt objects that we know of. Bigger than asteroids but not quite planets, dwarf planets are big enough to be rounded under the force of their own gravity but too small to clear their orbits like planets do. While the International Astronomical Union (IAU) has officially confirmed five dwarf planets — Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake — astronomers studying dwarf planets often recognize at least nine, with several more candidates whose properties are still unknown.

Depending on which astronomer you ask, there could be anywhere from a handful to hundreds of dwarf planets in this part of the solar system. Identifying which Kuiper Belt objects are dwarf planets is tricky because they are often very dim and move very slowly from Earth's perspective, since their orbits are so large and distant. The likeliest candidates have high albedo (surface reflectivity) and diameters greater than roughly 370 to 500 miles (600 to 800 km).

What makes ED138 special is its size, inferred from its brightness, albedo and distance from the sun. It's estimated to have a diameter between 370 to 930 miles (600 to 1,500 km). For comparison, Pluto — the largest dwarf planet recognized by the IAU — is 1,477 miles (2,377 km) in diameter. Ceres, the smallest IAU-recognized dwarf planet, is 595 miles (958 km) in diameter. Future observations of ED138 will give researchers a more accurate idea of its diameter and density to determine if it's round enough to join the dwarf planet club.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said in the statement. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

#6437. After the dinosaurs died, the massive ‘D. rex’ fungus ruled the woods

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Dianjunus rex’s mushrooms can be half a meter tall and weigh over two kilograms

Dianjunus rex (shown) grows in southwestern China and its yellowish, pillar and tentacle-shaped fruiting bodies may be the largest known among sac fungi.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A pineapple-sized fungus has quietly grown undetected in the forests of southwestern China – until now. The massive mushroom may set a size record for a major branch of the fungal family tree.

The fungus — named Dianjunus rex — may also represent a previously unknown family, researchers report September 28 in Frontiers in Fungal Biology. Fittingly, D. rex is part of a lineage that split off from other fungi right after the dinosaurs — like T. rex — went extinct.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2024, researchers in China were conducting a survey of fungal diversity in a tropical rainforest in Yunnan Province when local farmers tipped them off to an unusual fungus in the area. The farmers included photos, says Indunil Chinthani Senanayake, a mycologist at the Kunming Institute of Botany in China. Some of the farmers who’d made the discovery took a bite of the mystery fungus, Senanayake says, and the tipster “wanted to confirm whether it was edible or not.”When Senanayake and her colleagues went to the location, they found strange, yellowish, tentacle-like and spatula-like mushrooms growing out of decaying tree roots. These were some kind of ascomycete, or “sac fungi”. Sac fungi like morels, truffles and molds make their spores in microscopic bladderlike receptacles, unlike the bowling pin-shaped reproductive structures in club fungi, the group that includes most culinary mushrooms.The mushrooms we see growing out of the ground are called fruiting bodies and make the spore-producing cells for the often hidden or subterranean fungus. Most sac fungi have relatively small fruiting bodies. But the mushrooms growing off these mysterious Yunnan fungi were enormous, with some reaching 50 centimeters tall. The team took samples of the fungi back to the lab for further study and found that they weighed up to 2.2 kilograms. By their estimates, these are the largest spore-making fruiting bodies among all sac fungi.

Torda Varga — a mycologist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in Richmond, England who was not involved with the research — notes that some truffle species are known to get close to the bulk. D. rex appears to be the largest sac fungal fruiting body he’s aware of. “What I find particularly remarkable is that a fungus with such an enormous fruiting body appears to have remained scientifically undocumented until now,” says Varga, though he adds his experience has mostly been within Europe.

The researchers compared samples of the fungus’s DNA with those from other fungi to determine its evolutionary relationships. They found that it was a relative of species like candlesnuff fungus and dead-man’s-fingers, which make fruiting bodies only a few centimeters tall, but that it was probably in its own, unique family. The team gave the new species the name Dianjunus rex, referencing both the Latin “rex” for “king” and the ancient Dian kingdom of the region.

The team’s genetic analysis suggests D. rex’s family first evolved in the aftermath of the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous Period that wiped out the dinosaurs, some 65 million years ago. “During the dark, cold, postimpact years after the mass extinction, fungi that decompose dead organic matter could keep functioning better than light-dependent photosynthesizers,” Senanayake says.

Varga wonders if searching databases for bits of DNA shed into the environment could help uncover other members of D. rex’s royal family in the absence of physical specimens.

“Some of these [genetic] sequences might belong to previously undocumented relatives of Dianjunus rex,” he says. Finding these hidden species could tell researchers more about the biology and evolutionary history of this king of the sac fungi.

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

#6434. The Missing Engine Behind Quantum Computing Is Literally All Around Us

Scientists say they can corral up to 40 quantum-ready photons from everyday light, even at room temperature.

The answer to one of the biggest questions in quantum computing might have been all around us this whole time: light. In newly published research, a team of scientists from Louisiana and Mexico say they’ve found a way to corral up to 40 viable photons of light “at room temperature under high levels of noise and decoherence,” for use in quantum information crunching. If this finding is validated by further research and implementation, it could help move quantum computing closer to real life.

The paper was recently published in the peer-reviewed journal Advanced Science. The research starts from an understanding that quantum computing, or quantum information processing, is something fundamentally different from the paradigms we have today. The team explains in the paper how their field, reservoir computing, differs from the von Neumann setup that the vast majority of computers have now. Instead, it’s closer to a neural network, with “highly-interconnected quantum networks as reservoirs.”

In a von Neumann system, information marches through a central processing unit (CPU) almost on a ticker tape. One minuscule math problem at a time is crunched onto that ticker tape, then returned to its host area of the computer—like memory, hard drive, software, or your mouse—to be applied. Everything the computer does gets crunched, one math operation at a time, through the CPU. In a neural net, including a reservoir computer, multiple things can happen at the same time. The computing style is nonlinear, involving clouds of quantum particles.

If that setup sounds thrilling, you’ve now joined a large group of people who feel excited about it, even if they aren’t sure yet how it can be implemented. The industry is bottlenecked by logistics. There’s no general purpose quantum computer. “Scalability and fragility have long represented two major challenges to the practical realization of quantum technologies,” the team writes. But in their simulation, the scientists were able to extract little quantum pockets from everyday “classical” light sources, corralling reservoirs that they say show a marked improvement over classical computing.

“We demonstrate the potential of our platform to perform complex tasks by using random multiphoton reservoirs to map input signals into higher-dimensional spaces, which are then optimized by low-level neural networks,” the team writes. In other words, the simulation shows that the reservoir system can set up and explore functions, taking an input and turning out the function performed on that input, like an algebraic expression and then the integral of that expression.

The secret in this experimental setup is the Fock space, which lets scientists gather particles under one umbrella in order to study how they behave, mathematically. Once a number of particles within the classical light source are corralled in a special circuit, they can be used to do quantum computing, despite their “losses and noise.” Light is bent and manipulated at “room temperature,” which in quantum mechanics means above freezing.

This work is the next step down a path that has, so far, worked only in much smaller setups. “While these effects have been explored in the context of nanophotonic systems and quantum sensors, their implications for multiphoton quantum information processing have yet to be investigated,” the team explains. “These results highlight the robustness and scalability of hybrid quantum technologies against decoherence.”

#6433. Roller coaster safety is a matter of science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Extreme ride guidelines don't all reflect the latest findings

Current industry guidelines for roller coaster design don’t account for all the forces riders face on extreme coasters from previous decades. Hershey Park’s Fahrenheit, pictured here, briefly held the world record for steepness when it opened in 2008.

The first roller coaster in the United States to loop upside down tucked riders by twos into bench seats, secured them with a single seat belt and subjected them to an estimated 7.5 times the force of gravity (some say it was closer to 12 g). The Flip Flap Railway opened in New York City’s Sea Lion Park in 1895, where the roller coaster reportedly strained backs, wrenched necks and dazzled spectators until the park closed in 1902.

Now, roller coaster safety is in the news again. In September, three lawsuits were filed against Six Flags and ride manufacturer S&S Global, alleging that riders sustained “catastrophic” brain injuries on the roller coaster X2 at California’s Magic Mountain theme park. These are just the most recent cases related to the ride, filed after a CNN investigation found dozens of injuries on X2 leading to hospitalization, disability and death. On September 29, Six Flags announced X2 would shut down permanently even though it said the ride “consistently passed a multitude of safety tests.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Weeks later, the company said it would temporarily close another nine coasters across the United States and Canada after a man fell from his seat on the roller coaster Goliath and died at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags announced Oct. 24 that it would add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters, and a spokesperson told Science News that the company is “committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures.” But the incidents and closures are prompting new questions about coaster design and safety — particularly when they are operating correctly — and whether guidelines overlook crucial factors.

Roller coasters are not regulated at the federal level in the United States; each state has its own approach to their management. But an international technical group comprising over 1,000 industry professionals, the ASTM Committee F24 on Amusement Rides and Devices, publishes recommendations that are considered industry standards.

The first ASTM standards for roller coaster design were released in 1982. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission had been stripped of authority to regulate fixed-site amusement rides the year before. In the wake of this newfound freedom, it was a “roller coaster arms race,” says Brian Avery, an event and tourism management researcher at the University of Florida in Gainesville who studies risk and amusement ride safety protocols. The period was characterized by attempts to “build it taller, faster, longer.”

When X2, originally called X, opened in 2002, it was the world’s first fourth-dimension coaster. It catapulted people 60 meters high, traveling 122 kilometers per hour while its seats rotated independently on their own tracks. In the 24 years since, only 20 or so other fourth-dimension coasters have been built, and several have closed.

As roller coasters grew more extreme, injuries increased and were more publicized, sparking calls for further research and regulation.

Generally, roller coasters are quite safe. Out of 1.7 billion annual amusement park rides across North America, just 652 roller coaster injuries were reported in 2024 by parks choosing to share data. Studies suggest that riding a roller coaster is very unlikely to cause a brain injury, although most research on roller coaster brain impacts is about a decade or more old.

In 2002, a study used reported g forces from three roller coasters in a mathematical model to determine that their acceleration levels were below those predicted to cause head injuries. A 2017 study found brain effects on three roller coasters that were low on average, but “comparable with mild sports impacts,” like those sustained by heading a soccer ball, at their peak.

“The limiting of g forces alone might be an insufficient design criterion for roller coaster rides,” wrote the authors of the 2017 study.

In 2020, David Eager, a biomechanical engineer at the University of Technology Sydney, coauthored a paper on under-acknowledged forces affecting roller coaster safety, including jerk (the rate at which acceleration changes), snap (the rate at which jerk changes) and vibration.

“Roller coaster passengers need time to sense acceleration changes and adjust their muscle tension or suffer conditions such as whiplash,” Eager wrote.

The ASTM standards are exacting in some ways. Research conducted during the space race led to a 6g recommended limit on roller coaster acceleration exposure. However, ASTM doesn’t make recommendations about other types of motion on a roller coaster that might impact the neck, head and brain. It disregards forces lasting less than 200 milliseconds, no matter how intense.

But each tiny imperfection and variation in the circumference of the track — especially plentiful in coasters built before modern manufacturing techniques — causes a jolt, says Jurnan Schilder, a mechanical engineer and researcher who teaches roller coaster design at the University of Twente in Enschede, the Netherlands. He studies ways to create smoother roller coaster rides.

Schilder’s research suggests that at each track imperfection, “theoretically, you experience infinite jerk.” On a fourth-dimension coaster, he says, two sets of tracks mean double the variations. “Not only is the train sometimes shaking, but also the tilting mechanism is shaking.”

Research beyond rides also suggests intense and repeated rattling, jostling and vibration could meaningfully impact the brain. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends limiting the duration and intensity of whole-body vibration. In April, the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab, which studies the science of brain injuries, published an article suggesting some concussions experienced by baseball players may result from just milliseconds of vibration.

North Carolina high school student Kayleigh Bonner’s quest to understand her father’s death exposed similar risks. After her father, a retired U.S. Coast Guard surfman who captained boats through rough waves for 21 years, experienced symptoms of a brain injury and died by suicide, Kayleigh surveyed 77 other elite surfmen for a senior capstone project. She found that 89 percent of those she spoke to had some symptoms of brain injury likely caused by the intense, rapidly changing forces traveling through their bodies as their boats were tossed by waves. Her quest to understand her father’s death was written about in July in the New York Times, and soon after acknowledged by the Coast Guard.

Of course, professional baseball players and Coast Guard surfmen have more significant and prolonged exposure to these forces than occasional roller coasters riders. But as researchers discover more about how different kinds of motion impact the brain, safety standards seem to lag behind. Minimizing jerk and snap is “an important consideration,” Eager says.

The mounting roller coaster-related headlines have renewed scrutiny of both the existing coaster safety standards and the lack of federal regulation. U.S. Rep. André Carson, a Democrat from Indiana, has called to pass a bill he first introduced in 2025 that would create federal oversight of amusement rides. Since 1999, Democratic U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to regulate fixed rides, but the bills have consistently stalled.

The amusement industry has long opposed federal oversight. In 2010, Avery coauthored a paper asserting that “the industry needs to find a collective voice and establish consistent self‐regulating policies in order to curb the incidents rates and avoid federal regulation.”

But Schilder says: “It makes you wonder: Are the current safety standards sufficient?”

For modern rides, Schilder says he believes they are. Modern manufacturing techniques mean roller coasters designed and built today are much smoother than predecessors. ASTM standards that filter out brief but intense forces, like vibration and jerk, are likely fine for rides that don’t vibrate and jerk very much. But at many parks, the ambitious and intense rides born of the roller coaster arms race are still in place.

Riders are “flirting, if you would, with danger when they experience rides and devices. They know that they’re more likely than not going to be safe,” Avery says. The point is to be “right on the cusp.”
